2.title: The Mind of Christ: Humility, the Incarnation, and the Cross
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a church under pressure from outside. Chapter 2 turns to the pressure inside: rivalry, conceit and grumbling, the kind of thing that later surfaces in two named women who cannot agree (4:2). Paul’s answer is not a technique but a person. He sets before them the mind of Christ, in one of the Bible’s great passages on the incarnation (2:6–11): the Son, in the form of God, went down to a slave’s death on a cross, and God has exalted him to the name above every name.

Then come the consequences: work out your salvation, because God is working in you; stop grumbling and shine like stars. The chapter closes with the same mind in two ordinary men, Timothy and Epaphroditus.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Appealing to all they have received in Christ, Paul asks for unity and a humility that puts others first. The mind he wants is theirs in Christ, who though truly God emptied himself, obeyed to the point of death on a cross, and has been exalted as Lord, to the Father’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
What the Son Laid Aside, and What He Did Not

In verse 7 the emptying is explained by the taking of a servant’s form, so it is not subtraction but addition: the Son did not become less than God but took to himself a full human nature, veiling his glory and setting aside the free use of his rights. This is the faith the church confessed at Chalcedon in AD 451: two natures in one person, without confusion and without division.

Verses 10–11 raise a second question. Every knee bowing does not mean everyone is saved; the same letter speaks of opponents whose end is destruction (1:28; 3:19). Universal acknowledgement is certain; universal salvation is not taught here.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi had a status problem. Paul’s vocabulary, eritheia, selfish ambition, suggests the quarrel of 4:2 was about position more than doctrine. Into that he drops the deepest thing he knows: the one with the highest claim in the universe declined to press it.

Now: In most church conflicts the useful question is not whether you have a right, since you probably do, but what you intend to do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Philippians 2 contains a towering passage about Christ, and Paul uses it for an intensely practical purpose: unity and humility in the church (vv. 1–4). Christ Jesus, in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant and went down to a cross, and God has highly exalted him (vv. 5–11). So they are to work out their salvation, because God is at work in them, and to shine like stars (vv. 12–18). Timothy and Epaphroditus show the mind of Christ in action (vv. 19–30). The chapter moves from the throne of God to a sickbed in Rome, and insists that they belong together.

Any encouragement in Christ. Four “if” clauses, and not one of them is in doubt: closer to since there is than to if there happens to be. Paul is naming what they already possess and then presenting the bill. “Encouragement” (paraklēsis) is a word built from calling someone alongside: the strengthening that comes from union with Christ.

Comfort, participation, affection. “Comfort” (paramythion) is consolation, what you say quietly to someone who is grieving. “Participation” is koinōnia again, now applied to the Holy Spirit himself: shared life in the one Spirit. “Affection” is splanchna once more, the gut word of 1:8, and “sympathy” (oiktirmoi) is mercy that feels. These are not abstractions. They are the actual furniture of an ordinary Christian’s life.

No excuse for division. Here is the force of the argument. Paul is saying: you have all of this. You have been strengthened by Christ, comforted in love, made partners in the Spirit, and moved in your own inward parts by mercy. A church that had none of these things might be forgiven for fragmenting. A church that has all four and still cannot get along has not run out of resources; it has declined to spend them.

Complete my joy. Paul, who rejoices in prison, over rivals, whatever the verdict, says his joy is not yet full. One thing is missing. Not his release. Their unity. He would rather have a united church in Macedonia than an open cell door in Rome. “Same mind” is to auto phronēte, think the same thing, and phroneō comes about ten times in Philippians. This is a letter about how Christians think, because how they think decides how they treat one another.

Full accord. Four ways of saying it: the same mind, the same love, full accord, one mind. The repetition is a man leaning on a point, because there were tensions in the church (4:2). “Full accord” translates sympsychoi, soul-joined. It is possible to disagree with someone about a good deal and still be soul-joined to them, and to agree about everything and be nothing of the kind.

What if the other person will not be reconciled? You are responsible for your part, not theirs. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). So do what is yours to do: confess your own share of the fault without adding but, ask forgiveness, offer it freely, and speak to them directly rather than about them. If they refuse, keep your heart free from bitterness, go on praying for them, treat them with courtesy, and leave the door open. Sometimes a wise third person can help (Matthew 18:16). Unity is a gift of the Spirit you are to keep, not a result you can force; but you can make sure the wall is not being built from your side.

On a Tuesday. If a relationship in your church has cooled, begin not with what the other person did but with what you have received: encouragement in Christ, the comfort of his love, the fellowship of his Spirit, mercy you did not deserve. You are not asked to produce love from an empty account, but to spend from a full one: a word of encouragement, a kindness, a small act of mercy.

For worship. The Father, the Son and the Spirit have lived for ever in perfect oneness, without rivalry or envy, and they have drawn sinners into that fellowship. The oneness he asks of us is only the overflow of the oneness he is, and the oneness he died to create.

verseByVerse.quote: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Selfish ambition or conceit. The two roots of division, named exactly. “Selfish ambition” is eritheia, the word used of the rival preachers in 1:17: the self-seeking politician working a crowd. “Conceit” is kenodoxia: kenos, empty, and doxa, glory. Vainglory: the pursuit of a reputation with nothing behind it, wanting to be thought something more than wanting to be something.

How they talk. These two drive a great many church quarrels, and they very rarely announce themselves. Nobody in Philippi was saying I am pursuing empty glory. They were saying they had concerns about the direction of things, that certain people were not being listened to, that a principle was at stake. That is how eritheia always talks. It never uses its own name.

But in humility. Against them Paul sets tapeinophrosynē, lowly-mindedness. In classical Greek the root was mostly an insult, a slave’s trait; no self-respecting Greek aspired to it. The Old Testament had long praised the lowly before God, and Christianity took a word Greece used for a defect and made it a virtue, because it had seen something Greece had not: God on a cross.

Count others more significant. The verb (hēgeomai) means to reckon, to judge a thing to be so, the same verb used of Christ in verse 6, who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped”. Paul is asking them to do the sum the way Christ did it. This is an act of judgement, not a feeling, and you can do it on a Tuesday morning whatever you happen to feel.

Also the interests of others. “Look” (skopeō) is to keep your eye on. And Paul’s little word also guards this from becoming morbid. Your interests are real and you may attend to them. They are simply not the only ones in the room. A great deal of unhealthy Christian self-denial has been built by reading this verse as though that also were not there.

Does this mean I must let people walk all over me? No. Counting others more significant is a choice to serve, freely made, not a duty to be exploited. Jesus served his disciples and washed their feet, and he also rebuked them, refused the crowd that wanted to make him king, and walked away from those who tried to throw him off a cliff. Looking to another’s interests sometimes means saying no, because indulging someone’s sin is not seeking their good. And this verse never requires anyone to remain under abuse. An abuser’s real interest is repentance, not continued power over you; the vulnerable must be protected, and wrongdoing brought into the light and, where it is a crime, reported. Humility serves; it does not enable evil.

Is this not a recipe for low self-esteem? No, because Paul is not asking you to hold a low opinion of yourself; he is asking you to stop needing an opinion of yourself at all. Low self-esteem and pride are both preoccupied with self: one keeps saying I am nothing, the other I am something, and both are always checking the score. The gospel settles the score from outside. If God has accepted you in Christ, his verdict is in, and you are free from the endless work of proving yourself. The humble person is not the one who thinks least of himself, but the one who no longer needs to think about himself in every room he enters.

The difficult person. Think of the person in your church you find most difficult. Humility here is not pretending you find them easy, and it is not concluding they are a better Christian than you. It is deciding, before the next conversation, that what they need out of it matters more than what you want out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have this mind among yourselves. One short verse, and the letter turns on it. “Mind” is phroneō again, and here it is plural and corporate: think this way, together. It is about the atmosphere between people: what it feels like to be in that room, whose interests get raised in that meeting. Paul is describing the culture of a congregation, and he is about to ground it in the deepest thing he knows.

Which is yours in Christ Jesus. A translation question changes how the hymn is heard. Older versions read: let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus; that is, imitate him. The ESV reads: which is yours in Christ Jesus; that is, this is the mind that belongs to you because you are united to him. The second half has no verb, and translators must supply one. Both readings are true. The mind of Christ is our model and our possession.

Why the difference matters. Take the verse as pure example and the hymn becomes a mountain to climb: be as humble as God was, a command guaranteed to crush anyone who takes it seriously. Take it as union and the mind of Christ is a possession already given to you because you are in him: this is now the atmosphere of the place where you live; behave like it. That is Paul’s pattern everywhere. The command always rests on the gift, and reversing them turns the gospel into mere religion within a single sentence.

The Christ hymn. Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn, sung before Paul wrote, or composed by Paul himself: Christ’s descent (vv. 6–8) and his exaltation (vv. 9–11). It is among the earliest and highest statements of Christ’s deity, written within about thirty years of the crucifixion. And Paul reaches for the incarnation to settle a squabble, which tells you both how seriously he took the squabble and how practical he expected his highest doctrine to be.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can copy Christ’s atoning work. Nobody else empties himself from the form of God, and nobody else’s death redeems the world. We copy his attitude, and we can do even that only because his atoning work has joined us to him.

Can I really have the mind of Christ? How? Yes, if you are in Christ, because the Spirit who lived in him now lives in you, and we have the mind of Christ (1 Corinthians 2:16). It grows in three ways. First, by looking at him: in the Gospels, in this hymn, in the Lord’s Supper. We are changed into the likeness of what we behold (2 Corinthians 3:18). Second, by asking for it, since this is a work God delights to do (2:13). Third, by practising it in small decisions: choosing the lower seat, the hidden service, the other person’s good. You will fail often. But it is already yours to grow into, not a foreign mind to be manufactured.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn.

verseByVerse.quote: who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the form of God. The word is morphē. It does not mean shape or outward appearance in the way the English form can suggest; it most likely means the outward expression of what something genuinely is. To be in the form of God is to be God, showing. Everything that makes God God, his glory, his power, his holiness, his right to be worshipped, belonged to the Son before he came; he speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5).

Was. “Was” (hyparchōn) means existing: his continual state before the incarnation. Paul is not describing a man who was promoted. He is describing someone who was there first. And form will return in verse 7, where he takes the form of a servant. He who really was God really became a slave.

A thing to be grasped. Then the hinge of the whole hymn. The noun behind grasped is harpagmos, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; the root means to seize or snatch. Either he lacked equality with God and refused to snatch at it, or he possessed it and refused to exploit it for his own advantage. The line before has just said he was in the form of God, so most readers rightly take the second: he held it by right, and would not use it for himself.

The second Adam. The temptation Christ refused was not to become something he was not, but to use what he genuinely was for his own advantage. Adam, who was not God, grasped at being like God (Genesis 3:5). Christ, who was God, did not grasp. It was precisely the temptation of the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11): you are the Son of God, so use it, feed yourself, prove it, take the kingdoms now without the cross. He had every right and opened his hands.

Aimed at the quarrel. And that is why this verse is aimed straight at the Philippian quarrel. The question in a church fight is almost never whether I have a right here. Usually you do. The question is what you do with the right you have. Christ’s answer, holding the highest rights in the universe, was to decline to press them for himself. Anyone who has ever been genuinely wronged in a congregation knows how much that costs, and how little like weakness it is.

If Jesus is God, how can he be distinct from the Father? This is the mystery of the Trinity, and Scripture teaches both sides plainly. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), and the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully God, three persons sharing the one divine nature, distinct but never divided. The Son is not a part of God or a lesser god; he is equal with the Father in power and glory (the Westminster Confession 2.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3). In this hymn you can see both truths: he was in the form of God, and yet he obeyed the Father and was exalted by the Father. That obedience belongs to the work of salvation he freely took on as our Mediator; it does not make him eternally lower than the Father, whose glory he shares. We cannot fully understand how God is three and one, but we can worship, because this is how he has shown himself.

For worship. Before there was a world, the Son shared the glory of the Father. He did not need us, and he did not need to come. Where Adam grasped and fell, he opened his hands and stooped. The one who had a right to everything spent his rights on us, and is no less God for having done it.

verseByVerse.quote: but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But emptied himself. The verb is ekenōsen, to empty, pour out; from it theology gets the word kenosis, and it has been made to say things Paul did not say. Look at the sentence: there is no object. Paul does not write he emptied himself of his divinity, or of anything else. He writes that he emptied himself, and then explains how: by taking the form of a servant. The emptying is not subtraction. It is addition. He did not become less God; he took to himself a human nature, a body, a mother, a birth, and with it he set aside the privileges and glory he had a right to.

Veiled, not surrendered. What he laid aside was not deity but its independent exercise for his own benefit: the free use of what was his. The glory was veiled, not surrendered; it broke out on a mountain (Matthew 17:2) to show it had been there all along. The Son who holds the universe together grew tired (John 4:6), needed sleep (Mark 4:38) and asked questions, because he had taken a genuine human life and would live it genuinely, depending on the Father and the Spirit.

The form of a servant. The same word, form (morphē), as verse 6: he truly became a servant, as truly as he was God. Doulos, slave: the word from 1:1, where Paul introduced himself. Paul’s self-description was not modesty; it was imitation. In Philippi this would have sounded strange. The Greek world had stories of gods appearing in human shape, but they were disguises, and none told of a god choosing the slave’s place out of love. The Roman world had a ladder of status that every citizen spent his life climbing. Paul announces a God who came down the ladder, all the way, on purpose.

The likeness of men. “Likeness” (homoiōma) guards both sides. He was truly human, not God in a costume, like us in every way except sin (Hebrews 2:17; 4:15). And the word born carries its own astonishment: the one who was in the form of God arrived as every one of us arrives, helpless, unable to lift his own head. The rich one became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Where Christians differ: what did Christ empty himself of? Kenotic theories, held by some modern theologians, teach that the Son gave up some divine attributes, such as omniscience or omnipotence, when he became man. This commentary’s view: the Son did not cease to be God or lose any divine attribute; God cannot stop being God. He emptied himself by taking human nature and the role of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine rights for his own benefit. He remained fully God while becoming fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion or change (the Chalcedonian Definition of AD 451; the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). During his earthly life, he chose to depend on the Spirit and the Father. He was not less than God in the manger, and he was not less than man on the cross.

If Jesus was God, how could he not know the day of his return? Because he had two natures, divine and human, in one person. As God, the Son knows all things. As man, he had a true human mind that grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and knew what the Father gave him to know for his mission. When he said he did not know the day (Mark 13:32), he was speaking truly of his human knowledge. This is not a contradiction but the wonder of the incarnation: the eternal Son really did live a human life from the inside, with its limits, without ever ceasing to be what he always was. It means he understands our limits too.

On a Tuesday. Look for one task this week that only a servant would do: the job nobody notices, the service nobody will thank you for, the person nobody else wants to help. Do it quietly, and remember who did it first, and for whom.

verseByVerse.quote: And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Found in human form. Verse 7 brought him from God to man; verse 8 takes him from man to a criminal’s execution, each step lower than the last. “Form” here is schēma, outward appearance. He looked like any other man. There was no halo in Nazareth.

He humbled himself. “Humbled” (tapeinoō) is from the same root as the humility of verse 3. Having become one of us, he went on going down. And the verb is active and reflexive: nothing was done to him that he did not accept. At the arrest and the trial he looks entirely passive, but he is a man descending on purpose: no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

Obedient to the point of death. Obedient to the Father, all the way (Hebrews 5:8). Here is the eternal Son, in the work of salvation he had freely undertaken, submitting his human will to his Father’s in a garden at night: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). And his obedience is our righteousness. Every day of that obedient life was lived on behalf of people who had not obeyed.

Even death on a cross. We have made the cross jewellery, and it takes an effort to recover what it was. Crucifixion was designed not merely to kill but to degrade: public, naked, slow. It was reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals, and Roman citizens, like many in Philippi, could not normally be crucified. Cicero said the very word cross should be kept far from the eyes, ears and thoughts of a Roman citizen.

The floor of the universe. So follow the line all the way down. From the form of God, to the form of a slave, to death, to the death the empire kept for slaves and rebels. He began at the highest point there is and did not stop descending until he reached the lowest point available in the world he had made. And there is one more depth the Romans could not see: to hang on a tree was to die under the curse of God’s own law (Deuteronomy 21:23). He took that curse on himself, Paul tells the Galatians, to buy us out from under it (Galatians 3:13). That is the floor of the universe, and he touched it.

How can God die? God the Son did not stop existing, and the divine nature cannot die. But the Son had taken a true human nature, body and soul, and in that nature he truly died: his body was laid in the tomb and his spirit committed into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). Because the two natures belong to one person, Scripture can say that the one who was crucified is the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), and that God obtained the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). It was not a mere man standing in for God at the cross. It was God the Son, in our flesh, dying our death.

Why did he have to die, and on a cross? Because our sin deserved the curse, and he came to bear it in our place. God is holy and just; sin cannot simply be overlooked. At the cross the Father laid on his Son the penalty we owed, so that it could be lifted from us: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The manner of his death matters: the cursed death of the tree showed that he was carrying the curse of the law, and the shameful death of a slave showed how low love would go. This is penal substitution, and it is the heart of the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the cross was only an example of humility. It was the atoning sacrifice for sin, once for all. But it is also the supreme example, and Paul is using it to settle an argument in a small church about who gets deferred to. Set any grievance you are currently holding beside that descent and see whether it survives the comparison.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful form of Roman execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Highly exalted. “Therefore.” The hymn turns on that word, and the direction of travel reverses: everything from verse 6 has been descent; from here it is all ascent, and the second follows from the first. Jesus stated it as a law: he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). “Highly exalted” (hyperypsoō) is super-exalted: resurrection, ascension, enthronement at God’s right hand (Acts 2:33; Ephesians 1:20–21).

Who acts. Through the descent, Christ was the subject of every verb: he did not count, he emptied, he humbled. Now he is the object: God has highly exalted him. The Son did not lift himself. He went down as far as there is to go and left the raising to his Father, which is exactly what the people quarrelling in Philippi were failing to do. If you are busy exalting yourself, you have taken over the Father’s job.

The name above every name. Which name? Not Jesus in itself; that was a common name in first-century Palestine, and he had borne it from birth. Verse 11 tells us: the confession that is coming is “Jesus Christ is Lord.” Kyrios, Lord, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses to render the divine name, Yahweh, the name devout Jews would not even pronounce. What is given to the risen Christ is God’s own name.

Every knee should bow. Then the most audacious thing in the letter. The words echo Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD says, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance,” in a chapter of uncompromising monotheism: I am the LORD, and there is no other (Isaiah 45:5). Paul takes the homage that God there reserves exclusively to himself, and says it is given to Jesus. It is hard to imagine a higher statement about Christ.

In heaven and on earth and under the earth. The phrase sweeps the whole of created reality. In heaven: angels. On earth: humans. Under the earth: the dead, and perhaps demons. All creation, every rational creature, will bow.

Jesus Christ is Lord. This is one of the earliest Christian creeds: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3). In Philippi, a Roman colony, loyal subjects could call Caesar lord; to say Jesus is Lord was to say who really holds the throne.

To the glory of God the Father. The Son’s exaltation is not a rival to the Father’s honour but the means of it (John 5:23). There is no competition inside the Trinity, no jockeying for position, which is precisely the disease Paul is treating in the Philippian church. He has shown them a God in whom there is no eritheia at all, and asked them to live inside that.

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Some Christians, moved by the breadth of this vision, read it as meaning every person will eventually confess Christ willingly and be saved (universalism). This commentary’s view: every knee will bow and every tongue confess, but not all willingly or savingly. Some will confess in joyful worship; others will be compelled to acknowledge his lordship at the judgement (Romans 14:10–11; Revelation 20:11–15). Isaiah 45:24 adds that all who were incensed against him will come to him and be ashamed. The letter itself forbids the universalist reading: Paul has just spoken of the destruction of the opponents (1:28) and will speak of those whose end is destruction (3:19). This is the universal acknowledgement of Christ’s lordship, not universal salvation. Hell is real and eternal (Matthew 25:46). The question this passage puts to a reader is not whether you will acknowledge him, but when, and in which posture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became God at his exaltation. He was always in the form of God (v. 6). He was exalted as the God-man, the Mediator: the one who had always shared the Father’s glory now received, in his human nature too, the honour due to his finished work.

Did Jesus earn his exaltation? In a sense, yes, as the Mediator, and that is good news for us. The Son did not need to earn his divine glory; he always had it (John 17:5). But as the obedient man who finished the work the Father gave him, he was rewarded with exaltation, and he was exalted not for himself alone but as the head of his people. Where he has gone, we will follow. The reward of his obedience is given to all who are united to him: because he lives, we will live also.

What does it mean to confess Jesus as Lord now? It means saying freely now what everyone will say one day. Confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, and you will be saved (Romans 10:9). It is more than words. It means owning him as your rightful King: trusting him to save you, obeying him when it costs, letting his word overrule your preferences, and naming him openly before others. To bow now is joy and life. To bow then, without having bowed now, is shame. The knee that bends today will never be ashamed.

Is it presumptuous to say every knee must bow to Jesus? Only if Christians were claiming that their side had won. But the one before whom every knee bows is the one who knelt to wash feet and went to a cross for his enemies. His lordship is not the triumph of a religious party; it is the rule of the only one who has never misused power. And no Christian can boast about it, because every believer was once among the knees that would not bend, and bent only because grace bent them (1:29). The claim is not that we are better. It is that he is Lord, and that he is good.

On a Tuesday. One day every knee will bow; a Christian is simply someone who has begun early. That turns the ordinary places where Jesus is not yet obeyed, your money, your tongue, your screen, your plans, into the next territory of his kingdom, and bowing there is not humiliation but homecoming.
verseByVerse.note: The words echo a passage where the LORD says every knee will bow to him alone; Paul applies them to Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — Working Out What God Works In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now that Paul is absent, they are to go on working out their salvation with reverence, because God is at work in them. They are to stop grumbling and shine like stars in a twisted world, holding on to the word of life. Even if Paul’s life is poured out like a drink offering on their faith, he is glad, and they should share his gladness.
verseByVerse.theology:
God’s Work and Ours

The decisive word in verses 12–13 is the small conjunction between them. Paul does not say work, but remember God is working too; he says work, for God is at work. God’s working is the ground of our effort, not its rival, and it reaches beneath our obedience to our desires: he works in us both to will and to work.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had a good record of obedience, but it had been built with an apostle available. Now that he is in chains, the first sin he names is the wilderness sin of murmuring.

Now: For the believer who feels the gap between who he is and who he longs to be, verse 13 says the longing itself is God’s doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My beloved. “Therefore” ties this to the hymn: because Christ obeyed all the way down, and because God raised him, therefore work. They have been obedient. And Paul calls them beloved before he asks anything of them.

Much more in my absence. Their record was built with an apostle in the room. The real test is now, with him in a cell and unable to come. Obedience that requires supervision is not yet obedience; it is compliance.

Work out your own salvation. Three things need saying, because few verses have been more misread. First, work out is not work for. The verb katergazesthe means to carry a thing through to its finish, rather as a miner works out a seam of ore that is already in the ground. Nobody works for a salvation Paul has already told them God began and will complete (1:6). They are working out what has been worked in: letting the new life God has given show up in actual choices, the apology you make, the lie you refuse, the temper you hold (Colossians 3:9–10).

Together. Second, the pronoun is plural throughout; your own salvation sounds like a private project in English. Paul is addressing a congregation with a quarrel in it, and working out includes working out their life together, in unity: not an anxious solo performance but a body doing this work in one another’s company.

With fear and trembling. Third, fear and trembling is not terror of hell. Paul uses the same phrase of his own weakness in Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3) and of a slave’s service (Ephesians 6:5). It is reverent awe and humble dependence. The trembling is not the fear that God might drop you; it is the awe of discovering that the holy God is at work in you, and that you had better not be careless in his workshop.

God who works in you. Then verse 13 turns the whole thing on its head. Paul does not say work hard, but remember God is also working, as though the two were in competition, each taking a share. He says work, because God is working. God’s activity is the ground of ours, not its rival. The verb is energeō, to be at work, from which we get energy.

To will and to work. Not merely the power to obey once you have decided: the wanting too. God gives both the desire and the ability. Which means that the Christian who notices in himself a genuine desire to please God is looking at evidence of God at work, not at his own good character. The wanting was a gift before the doing was. And he does it for his good pleasure: because it pleases him to. You are not a project he took on reluctantly.

The power that raised him. Paul’s therefore reaches back to the hymn. Christ became obedient to the point of death (2:8), and their obedience is his being reproduced in them. The copy is never perfect, and it need not be: his obedience, not theirs, is counted as their righteousness (Romans 5:19), so their imperfect working out is accepted for his sake. And the God at work in them is the God who lifted the obedient Son from the cross to the throne: the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in every believer (Romans 8:11). So the desire to obey that you find in yourself this morning is God doing in you, in small, what he did at the empty tomb: making dead things live.

Where Christians differ: God’s work and ours. Sanctification means growing holy in practice: the lifelong process by which God makes a forgiven person more and more like Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Some say sanctification is all God’s work and we are passive; others that it is all our effort. This commentary’s view: both are fully true. God works in us; therefore we work out. Our working does not compete with his; it is the result of his. This is not cooperation as equal partners, but our real activity flowing from his prior and deeper work (the Westminster Confession 16.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.3). We pray as if everything depends on God, because it does, and work because God is working.

How do I know whether I am working out my salvation or just trying hard in my own strength? Look at where the effort is aimed and what it leans on. Effort in your own strength is anxious, proud when it succeeds and despairing when it fails, and it rarely prays. Working out what God has worked in begins in prayer, uses the means he gives (his word, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church), keeps going after failure because it rests on his promise and not on its record, and gives him the thanks when it succeeds. The test is not how hard you try but whom you are trusting while you try.

I feel the gap between who I am and who I long to be. Is God still working? Yes. If you feel the gap between the person you are and the person you long to be, that gap is not proof that God has left you to it. The longing itself is his. He is not standing at the end of the road waiting to see whether you make it; he is in you, this morning, producing both the appetite and the ability. Take the next small step of obedience in front of you, and thank him for the desire to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do all things without grumbling or disputing,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do all things without grumbling. A sin almost nobody repents of. “Grumbling” is gongysmos, a low muttering, the word the Greek Old Testament uses over and over for Israel in the wilderness: murmuring about the water, the food, the leadership (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10). And that murmuring lay at the heart of what kept them out of the land and turned a journey of weeks into forty years of funerals. God took it as an insult aimed past Moses at himself, because that is what it was.

Or disputing. “Disputing” (dialogismos) is the other half: the arguing, the questioning, the endless relitigating of decisions, quarrelsome arguments that divide. Grumbling is what happens in the car on the way home; disputing is what happens in the meeting.

All things. Paul allows no exception: not the genuinely annoying, not the decision that really was wrong. And the application of the Christ hymn, the thing Paul reaches for first after the throne and the cross and the name above every name, is: stop muttering.

The respectable sin. Grumbling is the sin of the respectable Christian: it never gets anyone disciplined, it feels like honesty, it can even be framed as discernment. But at its root it is a complaint about the way God is running things, delivered to a third party because it cannot be said out loud to him. And it comes precisely here, after God works in you, because grumbling is the natural response of someone who believes he is on his own with circumstances he did not choose. Paul does not tell them to cheer up; he tells them who is in the room.

The Son who did not murmur. Israel grumbled about bread in the wilderness for forty years. Jesus went into the wilderness for forty days, and when the tempter offered bread, he answered with the lesson Israel had failed to learn: man does not live by bread alone (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3). Where they muttered, he trusted his Father. A Christian who stops muttering is sharing the mind of the Son who trusted his Father in the desert.

Is all complaining sin? No. There is a difference between lament and grumbling. Lament takes the pain to God, honestly, even angrily, and ends in trust: how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1), and then, I have trusted in your steadfast love (13:5). Grumbling takes the pain to everyone except God and ends in bitterness. Lament is faith in distress; grumbling is unbelief in conversation. So weep, ask, and pour out your heart to him. What you must refuse is the muttering that hardens into a settled grievance against God or his people.

How do I raise a real concern without grumbling? Take it to God first and pray about it until your heart is not hot. Then take it to the person who can actually do something about it, not to everyone else (Matthew 18:15). Speak plainly and kindly, assuming good motives where you honestly can. Suggest a remedy if you have one, and offer to help. Then accept the outcome graciously, even if you still disagree, unless a matter of conscience or sin is at stake. A concern raised this way builds a church. The same concern muttered in the car park tears it down.

On a Tuesday. This week, each time you catch yourself muttering, stop and turn it into a prayer, and then into a thanksgiving for one thing God has given in the same situation.

For worship. The Lord bore with a murmuring people for forty years and never once stopped feeding them. His Son was silent before his accusers (Isaiah 53:7) and opened his mouth only to pray, to promise and to forgive. He took the wages of every complaint his people ever muttered against God, and from his silence came their peace.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blameless and innocent. Now the purpose, and it is a good deal larger than a quieter church. “Blameless” (amemptos) means no just cause for blame. “Innocent” (akeraios) means unmixed, pure, like wine not watered down or metal without alloy.

Children of God without blemish. “Without blemish” (amōmos) is what a sacrificial animal had to be to be offered at all. And he gives them a name before the description: children of God. It is not a title they must earn by being blameless. It is who they are, and blamelessness is the family likeness (1 Peter 1:15).

Without blemish because he was. The New Testament uses the phrase first of Christ: he offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14). Only one life has ever been fit for the altar on its own merits, and he has reconciled his people by his death, in order to present them holy and blameless before him (Colossians 1:22). So the call is not a demand to supply what only the Lamb could supply. It is a call to become in daily life what his sacrifice has already made them before God.

A crooked and twisted generation. A quotation from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5), where the crooked generation is Israel, God’s own people in the wilderness, murmuring. Paul applies it to the surrounding unbelieving world, having just warned the church against the very sin that earned Israel the label. The line is not drawn by ancestry. And note the preposition: in the midst. Believers live in the middle of it, not withdrawn from it.

Lights in the world. “Lights” is phōstēres, not the word for a lamp but the word Genesis 1:14–16 uses for the sun, moon and stars (compare Daniel 12:3). The picture is a small church in a Roman colony set into the dark like a star, visible for the same reason stars are visible: because it is dark. The darkness does not defeat the light; it is what makes it possible to see (Matthew 5:14–16).

A star does not lecture. And a star does not shine at people. It simply is what it is, and anyone who looks up can see it. Paul’s picture of Christian witness here is not primarily a message delivered but a community visible, which is why the command that produces it was about grumbling. A church that does not mutter is already preaching something to a city that does.

The word of life. The verb epechontes can mean holding fast or holding out. Both fit: the church clings to the gospel for its own life and holds it out to a world that has none. You cannot do the second for long without the first.

Not in vain. The metaphors are athletic and agricultural: the runner and the labourer. Paul admits frankly that on the last day he wants something to show for his life: not to be admired, but for his running not to have been for nothing. Their faithfulness will prove his work was not wasted. This is what a pastor’s ambition looks like when it has been converted: the people are the prize.

Should Christians withdraw from a corrupt world? No. Stars shine in the night sky, not in a bunker. Jesus prayed not that his Father would take his people out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). So stay in your workplace, your street, your school, your family. Be careful about what shapes you: guard your heart and choose your closest influences wisely. But do not mistake isolation for holiness. A light hidden under a basket has not been kept pure; it has simply stopped being a light.

How do I shine without being self-righteous? Remember that the light is borrowed. You shine as the moon does, by reflecting the sun, and you were part of the crooked generation yourself until God called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. So be honest about your own failures; humility is part of the shine. Be kind, generous, truthful and cheerful, especially in hard circumstances. Do not grumble about the culture as though you were better than it. And when people ask, be ready to point them to the source of the light rather than to yourself.

On a Tuesday. Think of the darkest place you will be this week: the office culture, the group chat, the family gathering. Decide one thing you will refuse to do there (join the grumbling, the gossip, the cynicism) and one thing you will do (an honest word, a kindness, a word about Christ if the door opens).

parallels.desc: those who are wise shall shine

verseByVerse.quote: Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A drink offering. Wine poured out with a sacrifice (Numbers 28:7): the last act, a small quantity, completing an offering someone else had brought. Paul pictures his possible death as his life poured out, and will use the image again when it has become a certainty: “For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come” (2 Timothy 4:6).

The offering of your faith. Paul is not the sacrifice. Their faith and service are the sacrifice (Romans 12:1), the main event on the altar; his own violent death, if it comes, is merely the cup of wine poured over the top. And it makes his execution an act of worship rather than a political accident. Rome thinks it is disposing of a troublemaker. Paul sees a priest at an altar. He is not being killed; he is being poured.

Poured out after him. Paul can speak calmly of being poured out because someone was poured out first. The Servant in Isaiah poured out his soul to death (Isaiah 53:12), and at the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and said that his blood was poured out for many (Mark 14:24). That pouring was the sacrifice itself, the one offering that takes away sin. Paul’s would be only a cup of thanks spilled beside it. A man who has drunk from the cup of the new covenant in Christ’s blood is willing, if God wills, to see his own life poured out on the same altar, and to call it joy.

Glad and rejoicing. Four verbs of joy in two verses, on the subject of his own execution. This is not stoicism, which grits its teeth and feels nothing, and it is not denial. It is the settled gladness of a man who worked the question out in chapter 1, to die is gain, and has nothing left to be afraid of.

Rejoice with me. The harder half: he tells them to rejoice with him, and anyone who has sat with a dying Christian more at peace than the family around the bed knows how demanding that is. Grief is not forbidden; he himself speaks of sorrow upon sorrow ten verses later. But he refuses to let the church treat his death as a defeat, because it is not one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s death atones for anything. Christ’s sacrifice is the only atoning sacrifice, offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). What believers offer is an offering of thanks, not of atonement: their faith, their service, their bodies, and if God wills, their lives.

Was Paul in fact martyred? Not at this point, it seems. He expected release (1:25; 2:24), and the letters to Timothy and Titus suggest he was freed and travelled again. Early Christian tradition says he was later imprisoned a second time and executed in Rome under Nero, in the mid-60s AD, by beheading, as a Roman citizen. 2 Timothy, written near the end, shows the drink offering finally being poured, and Paul still at peace: the time of my departure has come.

How can I rejoice when a Christian I love is dying? You do not have to choose between grief and joy; in a believer they can run together. Weep, because death is an enemy and parting hurts. And rejoice, because for them it is gain, and their life has been an offering God accepted. Tell them what their faith has meant to you. Pray with them, read them the promises, sing if they want to sing. Many Christians have found that the joy came not by forcing it but by looking at death from the dying believer’s side, as Paul asks, and seeing Christ waiting there.

On a Tuesday. Ask what in your ordinary life could be an offering to God: the work you will do today, the care you give a child or a parent, the money in your account, the hours of a hard week. Offer it to him in so many words this morning.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering was wine poured out with a sacrifice, completing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–30 — Two Men Who Show You the Mind of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul hopes to send Timothy, who shares his genuine care for them and has proved himself like a son serving with his father, and then to come himself. Meanwhile he sends back Epaphroditus, who nearly died serving Paul on their behalf, and asks them to welcome and honour him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Virtue Has to Be Seen in a Face

After the doctrine, Paul gives a person. Timothy embodies 2:4, looking to the interests of others, and Epaphroditus embodies 2:7–8, pouring himself out to the point of nearly dying. Neither is presented as exceptional. They are what the gospel ordinarily produces in people it has got hold of.

Paul also admits to sorrow, and to sorrow that could have been piled upon sorrow. Joy in this letter runs underneath sadness; it does not replace it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Epaphroditus was returning early, ill and with the job unfinished, and Paul heads off conclusions before the man reaches the gate: he is not coming back a failure but a soldier who gambled his life for Christ’s work.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be cheered by news of you. For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To send Timothy soon. After the hymn, travel arrangements. That is not an anticlimax; it is the point. Paul has set out the mind of Christ, and now he introduces two men in whom it can actually be seen. The Philippians did not need another idea. They needed a face. And even the itinerary is held inside Christ: Paul’s plans are in the Lord, held in a hand that may close on them (v. 23).

Cheered by news of you. The verb is eupsycheō, found nowhere else in the New Testament: to be good in soul. The man who rejoices in prison admits that he needs cheering up, and that news from this church would do it. Contentment in Paul is never self-sufficiency. He needed people.

No one like him. The key word is isopsychos, of equal soul, like-minded: nobody else of one soul with me. Timothy shares Paul’s heart. And what makes him unique is not his ability.

Genuinely concerned. “Genuinely” (gnēsiōs) comes from a root meaning true-born, legitimate: not the counterfeit article. Plenty of people can produce concern for a congregation when the situation calls for it. Timothy’s was the real thing. He embodies the humble mind Paul asked for, looking to the interests of others (2:4): the command walking about in a body, and a small copy of the Son who looked to our interests all the way to the cross (2:6–8).

The gift Paul could least spare. And there is a quiet rebuke in the arrangement, if the Philippians cared to notice it. Paul is sending them his most valuable colleague, the one man of his own soul, at the moment he is least able to spare him. A church arguing about who ranks where is about to receive, as a gift, the person its founder could least afford to give away.

If Christ is enough, why did Paul need cheering up? Because Christ is enough in a way that includes his people, not excludes them. God made us to need one another, and he often sends his comfort through them: God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus (2 Corinthians 7:6). Needing friends is not a failure of faith; it is how the body of Christ is designed. Paul’s joy in Christ was real, and so was his joy in good news from people he loved. If you are lonely and low, it is not unspiritual to say so, and it is not unspiritual to ask for company.

verseByVerse.quote: For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me, and I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all seek their own. A bleak sentence. He cannot mean literally every Christian in Rome: most of the brothers were emboldened (1:14), and Epaphroditus was faithful. He most likely means everyone available for this errand. Even softened, it should be allowed to stay hard. The apostle to the Gentiles looked around for someone who would put a distant congregation ahead of his own convenience, and found one man.

Their own interests. Paul does not say they sought sin; he says they sought their own interests, the phrase from verse 4. These were not scandalous people. They were ordinary Christians with their own things to be getting on with, and that was enough to disqualify them. Self-interest does not need to be dramatic to be deadly.

The interests of Jesus Christ. The hymn has just said what they are: he did not please himself (Romans 15:3), but gave himself for people who had no claim on him. So seeking his interests is not adding a religious hobby to a busy life. It is caring about what he cares about: a distant congregation’s welfare, the weak brother, the progress of the gospel. Timothy’s concern for the Philippians was the shape his devotion to Christ took.

Proven worth. Dokimē: tested character, metal that has been through the assayer’s fire. Not promise or potential, but what has been tested, and the Philippians had watched it happen (Acts 16:1–3).

As a son with a father. Then Paul’s grammar slips, beautifully. He begins as a son with a father, and cannot finish it that way, because it would require him to say he served me. So he changes course mid-sentence: he served with me in the gospel. Not under Paul: alongside him, both of them slaves (douleuō) of the same Master. The stumble tells you more about how Paul regarded this younger man than a paragraph of praise would.

As soon as I see. Verses 23–24 close the plan and quietly reveal Paul’s state of mind. The trial is still undecided, and he wants Timothy to be able to carry definite news after the outcome is known.

I myself will come. He expects release, as he reasoned in 1:24–25, and the confidence is carefully hedged, I trust in the Lord, by a man who might be poured out as a drink offering (2:17). He holds both without strain, which is what hope looks like when it has stopped needing certainty.

How do I know if I am seeking my own interests rather than Christ’s? Look at the ordinary choices, because that is where these Christians failed. When a need arises that would cost you time or comfort, what is your first reaction? Do you serve only where you will be seen or thanked? Are your plans for the year shaped by what will advance Christ’s kingdom, or only by what suits you, with Christ fitted in around the edges? Seeking his interests does not mean neglecting your family or work; those are part of his interests. It means asking, before you decide, what would serve him and his people, and being willing for the answer to cost you.

How do I find a Timothy, or become one? Spiritual fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, are formed by shared life, not just shared classes. If you are older in the faith, look for a younger believer and invite them alongside you: to pray with you, to serve with you, to see how you handle real situations. If you are younger, ask a mature Christian whether you can spend time with them and learn. Paul took Timothy on his journeys (Acts 16:3). Proven worth is built over years of faithfulness in small things, watched by someone who loves you enough to tell you the truth.

On a Tuesday. A diary is an honest confession: it shows whose interests filled last week. Somewhere in your week is a task nobody wants, a visit, a gift, an hour of prayer for missions, that could be done purely for the interests of Jesus Christ. And think of a Christian carrying a heavy load, and send them good news this week; you may be the cheer they need.

verseByVerse.quote: I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, for he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed he was ill, near to death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphroditus. Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul (4:18). Now Paul sends him home, probably carrying this letter. He had probably been sent to stay and serve; he is coming home early, ill and empty-handed, and everyone in Philippi will have a view about that. So Paul, before the man arrives, builds him a reputation. He is not returning a failure. He is returning a soldier.

Brother and fellow soldier. Five titles in one sentence, and they climb. Brother, family; fellow worker, the same task; fellow soldier, the same danger, and that is not decorative, since the man nearly died getting to Paul.

Messenger and minister. Then the two that belong to the Philippians. “Messenger” is apostolos, sent one: their envoy. “Minister” is leitourgos, priestly servant, from the same root as the offering of verse 17. Their gift, carried by this man, was an act of worship.

Distressed for them. He was near death, and the thing that troubled him was not his own condition but the knowledge that the news had reached home and they would be worried. The word for distressed (adēmoneō) is a strong one: deeply troubled, the word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). Here is the mind of Christ at the level of a sickbed: a dangerously ill man whose distress was for the people who were distressed about him.

God had mercy on him. Paul refuses to dress it up: seriously ill, with no hint that the illness was a failure of somebody’s prayers. The recovery is credited entirely to mercy. And Paul extends the mercy to himself, lest he should have sorrow upon sorrow: the man who wrote to die is gain admits that he was already carrying sorrow, and that losing this friend would have piled more on top. Grief is not unbelief. Paul’s joy was never the absence of grief; it ran underneath it.

Why did Paul not simply heal him? Because even the apostles could not heal at will; the signs were God’s to give, not theirs to command. An apostle who healed people elsewhere (Acts 19:11–12) here watched his friend nearly die and could not stop it, and he also left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). The miraculous gifts were signs given through the apostles to confirm the gospel in its foundation (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and we hold, charitably towards brothers who see it otherwise, that such sign gifts have ceased, while God still heals in answer to prayer as he wills. Many faithful Christians and whole churches that pray for healing and practise spiritual gifts read these passages differently, and they are our brothers and sisters in Christ. So Christians today should pray for the sick in faith, use the means God gives, including medicine, and leave the outcome to his mercy, as Paul did here.

What it does not mean. It does not mean healing is automatic for those with faith. And it does not mean that when a believer is not healed, God has been unmerciful or someone’s faith was weak. Sometimes God’s mercy is recovery; sometimes it is taking his child home, which is far better (1:23).

Is it unspiritual to be deeply distressed, or even depressed? No. Epaphroditus was deeply troubled; Paul expected sorrow upon sorrow; Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane and said his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Mark 14:33–34). Strong emotion, even overwhelming distress, is not in itself sin or a lack of faith. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmists did. Let other believers help you carry it. And if low mood persists or deepens, seek help from your doctor as well as your pastor: the body and the mind are both God’s creation, and using medical help is no more unspiritual than Paul’s concern for Epaphroditus’s recovery.

On a Tuesday. If someone in your church is ill, bring them to God specifically, and visit, call or write this week. And if you are the one who is ill, let people care for you; that, too, is part of the fellowship of the body.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The more eager. One verse of travel arrangement, and a very human one. The word for eager carries urgency: Paul is hurrying. He is not waiting for a convenient moment or for his own affairs to settle, which is very likely why this letter was written when it was: it went in the hand of a man who needed to go home.

Less anxious. Literally, less sorrowful. The man who will write do not be anxious about anything (4:6) has entirely real cares, a friend’s health, a frightened congregation, a capital trial with no date on it, and does what he can to reduce them. Freedom from anxiety in Paul is never the absence of things worth worrying about, but what a man does with them.

The mind of Christ in a travel plan. He needs Epaphroditus; they need to see him alive; so he sends him (2:4). Christ’s mind is seen when a prisoner gives away the friend sent to care for him so that a church can stop grieving.

Protecting a servant’s reputation. He explains the return twice, in verse 26 and here, so that nobody in Philippi can assemble a story about a man who gave up and came home. Protecting a servant’s reputation before he arrives is an unglamorous kind of love, and every church needs it.

How can Paul be anxious and yet tell me not to be? Because there are two different things under the same English word. Concern is the right weight of love for people and situations God has given you: Paul speaks elsewhere of his daily anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). Sinful anxiety is fretting that takes the burden away from God and carries it alone, imagining the worst and trusting nothing. Paul’s way was to feel the concern fully, pray about it, do the practical thing within his power, and leave the rest with God. That is exactly what 4:6–7 commands. You will still feel concern; the question is where you take it.

verseByVerse.quote: So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and honor such men, for he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to complete what was lacking in your service to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Receive him with all joy. Paul is still managing the homecoming. He wants no cool reception at the gate, no disappointment that he came home early, no unspoken question about why. Welcome him with all joy, and do it in the Lord: as a brother in Christ, not as an employee who failed to complete his contract.

Honour such men. Then a wider instruction: make it your policy to hold people like this in honour. That is pointed, said to a church with a status problem. Paul has spent the chapter dismantling the pursuit of empty glory, and he does not finish by abolishing honour. He redirects it: to the man who nearly died on an errand and has nothing to show for it, not to the impressive, the gifted or the visibly successful.

Risking his life. Paraboleuomai, a gambler’s term: staking, throwing your money onto the table. He staked his life. (The KJV’s not regarding his life follows later manuscripts with a similar-looking word.) Centuries later in Alexandria a brotherhood of Christians who nursed the sick, plague victims among them, was called the parabolani, a name usually traced to the same root: not recklessness, but a deliberate bet that a life is worth staking on Christ’s work.

What was lacking. Not a rebuke. The Philippians had given generously; what was lacking was the one thing they could not send: themselves. Epaphroditus went in their place, filling the gap with his own body. He was their hands, arriving where they could not.

The chapter ends on the ground. It opened with the Son of God taking the form of a slave; it closes with an unremarkable Christian from a provincial church gambling his life to carry a gift to a prisoner. Paul puts him in the same chapter as the Son of God, and means the comparison. The mind of Christ is mostly worked out by people whose names would otherwise never have been recorded.

How should we honour people like this without creating celebrities? Honour them in the way Paul does here: welcome them warmly, speak well of them, tell their story truthfully so that people praise God for them, care for their needs, and listen to them. Honour the quiet servants especially: the carer, the volunteer, the missionary back from a hard place, the believer who lost a job for the faith. Honour should point beyond them to Christ, whose work they did. The danger is not honouring people but honouring the wrong things in them: gifts and visibility instead of faithfulness and sacrifice.

What does risking for Christ look like for an ordinary Christian? For some it is literal: believers in hostile countries, missionaries in dangerous places, doctors and nurses who serve where disease is rife. For most of us it is smaller but real: risking a friendship by speaking about Christ, risking a career by refusing to lie, risking comfort by caring for someone who is difficult or ill, risking money by giving generously. Epaphroditus did not seek danger; he took on a task for Christ and did not let the danger stop him. Ask not how to be heroic, but what task Christ has given you that you have been avoiding because it might cost you.

For worship. Christ staked everything, knowing exactly what it would cost, and paid it in full. He went in our place where we could not go, and supplied with his own body all that was lacking in our service to God. One day he will say, well done, to people nobody else ever thought to praise.
