3.title: Knowing Christ: The Surpassing Worth and the Pressing Forward
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a warning and a testimony. Travelling teachers were telling Gentile believers that faith in Christ was not enough: they must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. His answer is his own life story. If anyone could have earned God’s approval by pedigree and performance, it was Saul of Tarsus, and all of it he now counts as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him with a righteousness from God through faith.

Then he guards against the opposite error: he has not arrived, but presses on like a runner because Christ has taken hold of him. He warns of enemies of the cross ruled by their appetites, and reminds the citizens of a Roman colony that their real citizenship is in heaven, from where they await a Saviour who will transform their bodies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Everything I Had, and What It Was Worth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul calls them to rejoice in the Lord and warns them sharply against teachers who insist on circumcision. Paul had every credential and now counts it all loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ and being found in him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification: A Righteousness From Outside

The decisive word in verse 9 is own. Paul does not want his law-righteousness at all. Against it stands a righteousness that comes from God and is received through faith, Christ’s record credited to those who are in him. A standing that rests on his record is the same on your worst day as on your best.

Verse 11 should not be read as doubt. By any means possible is openness about the route, not uncertainty about the destination.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers offered the Philippians a supplement: faith plus circumcision, grace plus performance. Paul’s answer is autobiographical: he held the complete set, more of it than any of them, and beside Christ it went out with the kitchen refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Philippians 3 is Paul’s testimony of what it means to know Christ, set against trust in religious achievement. He warns against teachers who insisted on circumcision: believers in Christ are the true circumcision, who worship by the Spirit, boast in Christ and put no confidence in the flesh (vv. 1–3). His own credentials were impeccable, yet he counts them all loss, even rubbish, beside the surpassing worth of knowing Christ and being found in him with a righteousness from God through faith (vv. 4–11). He has not arrived, but presses on like a runner toward the upward call of God in Christ (vv. 12–16). Against the enemies of the cross he sets a citizenship in heaven and a Saviour who will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body (vv. 17–21).

Finally, my brothers. “Finally” does not mean Paul is winding up: two chapters remain, and the sharpest passage in the letter is about to begin. The phrase (to loipon) means as for the rest: a hinge, not a conclusion (1 Thessalonians 4:1). Theories that chapter 3 was once a separate letter have no manuscript evidence; the change of tone is explained by the danger Paul is about to name.

Rejoice in the Lord. It is a command, as again in 4:4, and you cannot order someone to feel something. The answer is in the words that follow the verb. The command is not be cheerful; it is rejoice in the Lord, and that names an object, not a mood. Paul is telling them to look at someone, on the reasonable assumption that joy will follow the looking.

The place you stand. The object is not his circumstances (a cell and a pending capital charge), nor the health of the church (which has a quarrel in it), nor the absence of enemies. Christian joy is not the conclusion you reach after surveying your situation; it is the place you stand while you survey it. And it is the keynote of the letter for a reason: joy in Christ is the protection against the false teachers he is about to warn of. Those who rejoice in Christ do not need anything else added to him.

A Lord who was bound. Who is the one we are told to look at? In this letter the Lord is Jesus, the one before whom every knee will bow (2:11). That is what makes the command reasonable. Joy in the Lord is joy in a person who emptied himself, went to a cross, and was raised and exalted (2:6–11). And he knows the place Paul writes from. He too was arrested and bound (John 18:12), brought before a Roman governor and condemned, and none of it unseated him as Lord. A prisoner can rejoice in such a Lord, because his chains are not the end of his story, any more than his Lord’s were.

The same things. He may mean the call to rejoice, or the warning that follows, which he says in verse 18 he has often told them before. Either way, the principle cuts against the preacher’s fear of being boring. It costs him nothing, no trouble to me, and it protects them: the word is asphales, safe, secure. Repetition is not the teacher’s failure of imagination. It is the handrail on the stair. (Compare 2 Peter 1:12–13.)

How do I rejoice in the Lord when I feel nothing, or feel low? Begin with the object, not the feeling. Rejoicing in the Lord starts as a decision to turn your attention to him: to read about him, to remember what he has done, to sing or say back to him what is true. Feelings often follow slowly, and sometimes they lag a long way behind. The psalmists show the way: why are you cast down, O my soul? Hope in God (Psalm 42:5). They talked to their own souls. Joy in Scripture can sit alongside tears, illness and grief; it is a settled gladness in God rather than a constant mood. And if low mood is deep and lasting, it is no failure of faith to seek medical help as well. God uses both.

Why do I need to hear the same truths over and over? Because we forget, and because the truths that matter most are deep enough never to be exhausted. Say that to anyone who has ever sat through a sermon on a text they already knew and felt vaguely cheated. The things a Christian most needs to hear are almost never new. They are the same handful of truths, driven in again, because we leak. Paul knew that about the Philippians and he knows it about us, and he refuses to be too sophisticated to say a thing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look out for the dogs. The tone changes without warning. Three times in one verse: blepete, look out, and three names for the same people, each calculated to sting. Dogs were half-wild scavengers on the rubbish heaps, and dog could be a Jewish insult for a Gentile: the outsider, unclean. Paul turns the word round. The people insisting that Gentiles must be circumcised to belong, the Judaizers, are themselves the dogs: they are the ones outside, scavenging at the edge of a covenant they have not understood.

Look out for the evildoers. Literally the evil workers. They prided themselves on works of the law; Paul calls their works evil, because works offered as a ground of acceptance with God are not obedience but rivalry with Christ.

Those who mutilate the flesh. Here is a pun that does not survive into English. Circumcision is peritomē, a cutting around. Paul calls what they practise katatomē, a cutting down, a hacking; and the verb behind it is used in the Greek Old Testament for the pagan gashing that the law forbade (Leviticus 21:5; 1 Kings 18:28). His point is that a sign severed from the thing it signified is no longer a sign. Insist on the knife as a condition of salvation, and what remains is not a sacrament but surgery.

For we are the circumcision. Not we are the spiritual equivalent of it: we are it. A congregation of Macedonian Gentiles, most of them uncircumcised, is told they are the covenant people, and the men pressing the knife are not. Believers in Christ, Jew and Gentile, are the true circumcision: circumcised in heart by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29). God himself has cut away the hard heart and given a new one (Ezekiel 36:26), as the prophets had promised: the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Worship by the Spirit. Paul defines the true circumcision by three marks, which together make a fair test of any church or any soul. First, they worship by the Spirit of God. “Worship” (latreuō) is the word for the temple service. To worship by the Spirit is to depend on the one who opens our eyes to see Christ and moves our hearts to love God, not on ritual or technique (John 4:23–24). So a plain prayer from a believing heart at a kitchen table is true worship, and a flawless ceremony from a heart that trusts itself is not. (The KJV’s worship God in the spirit follows later manuscripts; the earliest read by the Spirit of God.)

Glory in Christ Jesus. Second, the boast has moved outside the self altogether. “Glory” (kauchaomai) is to boast, and the true circumcision boasts in one person only (Galatians 6:14), the one the sign pointed to. Paul tells the Colossians that believers were circumcised by the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11), and many take this as his death on the cross, where the body of flesh was put off. The Judaizers were pressing on Gentiles a cutting that pointed to a death Christ had already died for them. To glory in Christ Jesus is to stop offering God your own cut and to rest in his.

No confidence in the flesh. Third, and this one searches us, because flesh here is broader than circumcision. It means human status, achievement and religious performance: everything about you that could be offered as a reason God should accept you. Your family, your record, your usefulness, the fact that you have never done anything disgraceful. The question is not whether you have such things but whether any weight is resting on them, and the honest way to find out is to notice what happens inside you when one of them is taken away.

What it does not mean. Paul was not anti-Jewish: he loved his people and could wish himself cut off for their sake (Romans 9:1–5). He opposed making circumcision a requirement for salvation, which turned grace into Christ plus something.

Is such harsh language ever right for Christians today? Rarely, and only in Paul’s kind of case. Jesus called the Pharisees “You serpents, you brood of vipers” (Matthew 23:33), and Paul uses strong words of those who corrupt the gospel (Galatians 5:12). But both reserve them for false teachers who lead others astray from the way of salvation, not for honest doubters, opponents in ordinary disputes or weaker believers. The rule for ordinary correction is that the Lord’s servant must be kind to everyone, correcting his opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). Sharpness has its place when the gospel itself is under attack, and even then it must not become contempt or the pleasure of a fight.

Where Christians differ: does we are the circumcision mean the church has replaced Israel? Some read it that way; others hold that Israel as a people still has a distinct future in God’s purposes. Paul means that all who worship by the Spirit and trust in Christ, Jew and Gentile alike, are the true people of God, the reality to which circumcision pointed. He does not say here that the Jewish people have no further place in God’s purposes; elsewhere he insists that they are still beloved for the sake of their forefathers (Romans 11:28), and Christians hold different views about how that future will unfold. What is clear is that there is one people of God in Christ, and Jewish people are welcome in it, and need Christ to enter it, on the same terms as everyone else.

Who are the Judaizers today? Anyone who says: Christ, plus something, is needed for you to be right with God. Today it is rarely circumcision. It may be a ritual, a church membership, a set of rules about food, dress or days, a particular spiritual experience, a level of commitment, or a list of good works. Any of these can be good in their place. The danger comes when one of them is made a condition of acceptance with God, or a badge of being a real Christian. Then Christ is no longer enough, and the gospel has been changed. Watch for it in your own heart, too, where it is quieter and more dangerous.

On a Tuesday. Finish this sentence honestly: God accepts me because Christ died for me, and because I… If anything comes after the and, that is where your confidence in the flesh is hiding. Bring it to God, set it down, and thank him that Christ is enough.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a Jewish insult for Gentiles; Paul turns it on those insisting on circumcision. “Mutilate” plays on the word for circumcision. A pun: “those who mutilate the flesh” (katatomē) versus “the circumcision” (peritomē) in v. 3.

verseByVerse.quote: though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reason for confidence. If anyone could trust in religious credentials, Paul could, more than the Judaizers. He outranks them on their own terms, so no one can say he rejects what he never had. Seven credentials follow, in two halves: four inherited, three achieved.

Circumcised on the eighth day. The first four were done to him before he had any say. Circumcised on the day the law required (Leviticus 12:3): not a convert circumcised as an adult, but born into the covenant.

The tribe of Benjamin. Benjamin is a real boast. It gave Israel her first king, Saul, whose name Paul carried, and alone stayed with Judah when the kingdom tore in two.

A Hebrew of Hebrews. Probably a Hebrew-speaking son of Hebrew parents: though raised in the Greek city of Tarsus, his family had kept the language and the ways when it would have been easier to let them go.

A Pharisee. Then three things he achieved. The Pharisees were the strictest party (Acts 23:6; 26:5): not the sneering caricature, but the most rigorous and respected school in Judaism, men devoted to obeying God in the detail.

A persecutor of the church. He offers this as a credential. His zeal for God’s law drove him to persecute those he thought were betraying it (Acts 8:3; Galatians 1:13–14). On the old accounting his worst act was his best qualification.

Blameless. He is not claiming sinlessness. Measured by outward law-keeping, as people saw it, no one could fault him: the record any neighbour in Tarsus or Jerusalem could inspect. That is the horror of his position: this man kept the rules impeccably and was, at the same time, a fierce enemy of the Son of God. Blamelessness had not made him good. It had made him dangerous.

The one blameless Israelite. Set Paul’s list beside the Lord he now serves. Jesus too was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), born of Israel and under the law (Galatians 4:4), though of Judah rather than Benjamin (Hebrews 7:14). But his blamelessness was not the outward kind a neighbour could inspect. He could ask his enemies, “Which one of you convicts me of sin?” (John 8:46), and no answer came. And where Saul’s zeal drove him to destroy others, Jesus’ zeal for his Father’s house consumed himself (John 2:17). Paul can throw his own record away because there is a perfect one, and it belongs to the one in whom believers are found.

Is it wrong to be thankful for my Christian upbringing, my church or my heritage? Not at all. Paul elsewhere lists Israel’s privileges with gratitude (Romans 9:4–5), and Timothy’s faith was first in his grandmother and mother (2 Timothy 1:5). A godly home, good teaching and a faithful church are great gifts. The danger is only in trusting them. Thank God for them as means he used to bring you to Christ, and then make sure your confidence rests on Christ himself and not on the gifts. A Christian heritage cannot save you, and the lack of one cannot keep you out.

Does this say anything to someone who is not religious? Yes, because everyone keeps a list. The irreligious version simply has different entries: I am a decent person, I work hard, I am honest, I am more tolerant than the religious people I know. Paul’s word flesh covers all of it, because it means anything about you that you offer as the reason you are acceptable. The moralist trusts his record and the free spirit trusts his goodness, and both are standing on the ground Saul stood on. The gospel says the same thing to each: the record that counts is not yours, and it is offered to you freely in Christ (v. 9).
verseByVerse.note: Benjamin was the tribe of King Saul, Paul’s namesake. “Hebrew of Hebrews” may mean he was raised speaking Hebrew or Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ
verseByVerse.commentary:
Counted as loss. Now the ledger, in the vocabulary of the counting-house. “Gain” (kerdos) is profit. The verb count (hēgeomai) is the one used in chapter 2 of the mind of Christ, who did not count equality with God something to exploit. Paul applies the same reckoning to his own assets and moves every one across the page. And the tense is perfect: a decision made and still standing, from the day of his conversion.

Everything as loss. First the past tense, the Damascus road when the books were rewritten; now the present tense, and the category has widened from his credentials to everything. That first verdict was not a young convert’s enthusiasm; nearly thirty years later he is still saying it, and saying it wider.

The surpassing worth. This is not a man who decided his old life was worthless and therefore turned to Christ. It runs the other way. Everything on that list was genuinely valuable: the covenant, the law, the zeal, all of it real gain. What happened was that he met something beside which they could not hold their value. “Surpassing worth” (hyperechon) is that which outranks. Bring a lamp into a room at night and it is a genuine treasure; carry it outside at noon and you would put it down and forget it. Nothing has happened to the lamp.

My Lord. This singular, personal phrase about Christ appears almost nowhere else in his letters. Whatever else the Damascus road did, it left this man with a person he could call his own.

The loss of all things. It was not only an accountant’s reckoning. Paul really lost: status, career, friends, perhaps family, comfort and safety. The man who had been a rising star of the Pharisees became a hunted itinerant who was beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and imprisoned (2 Corinthians 11:23–27).

Rubbish. Then the language turns violent. Skybala is not a polite word, and rubbish is a translator’s kindness. It meant scraps thrown to the dogs, and, in its coarser use, dung. Paul has just called his opponents dogs; now he says his own pedigree belongs on the rubbish heap where they scavenge. He chooses the strongest word available. Compared with Christ, the most impressive religious record is garbage.

That I may gain Christ. It is the man who found treasure hidden in a field and in his joy sold all that he had and bought it (Matthew 13:44–46). The man is not grimly sacrificing. He is getting a bargain.

Does counting everything as loss mean I should despise my family, my work or the good things of life? No. Paul counts them as loss in comparison with Christ and as a ground of standing before God, not as worthless in themselves. Elsewhere he says that everything created by God is good, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4), and he commands husbands to love their wives and parents to care for their children. The point is ranking, not rejecting. When Christ is first, every other good thing finds its proper place and is enjoyed more, not less, because it is no longer asked to carry the weight of a god. What must go is whatever competes with him.

How do I come to value Christ like this? Not by trying to despise other things, but by seeing more of him. The lamp is put down because the sun has risen. So spend time looking at Christ in the Gospels and the letters; ask God to open your eyes to his worth (Ephesians 1:17–18); sing about him; listen to believers who love him. And watch what happens when you lose something precious and still find him there: that is often when people discover his worth most deeply.

On a Tuesday. Think back to the last time your career, your family name or your reputation for soundness was threatened, and ask whether the loss felt like the loss of a lamp at noon, or like the end of the world. If it was the second, you are not disqualified; you have been shown where to look. Tell Christ today what he is worth to you, and ask him to make it truer.

verseByVerse.quote: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith—
verseByVerse.commentary:
And be found in him. This verse is the doctrinal centre of the letter. Found by whom, and when? On the day of Christ, the day this letter keeps returning to (1:6, 10; 2:16). Paul imagines the final inspection, and his entire strategy for it is to be discovered inside someone else: united to Christ, sheltered in him. Not beside Christ with his own record in his hand, but in him. Faith joins a believer to Christ so closely that what belongs to Christ is counted as his: Christ’s death for sin, and Christ’s obedience, which becomes his righteousness (Romans 6:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

A righteousness of my own. Two kinds of righteousness. The first is my own: produced by my law-keeping and effort. The crucial word is own. He is not saying his law-righteousness fell a little short; he was outwardly blameless. He does not want it. It is the wrong kind of thing altogether: not a small coin but a forged one, and the trouble with a forged coin is not that it is small.

Pride or despair. A righteousness of your own can only ever produce one of two results, and both are fatal. If you think you have achieved it, it makes you a Pharisee, and Paul has just shown you what that produced in him. If you know you have not, it crushes you.

Through faith in Christ. The other righteousness is received through faith in Christ. The ESV note mentions through the faithfulness of Christ. Faith in Christ is the better reading, as in Galatians 2:16, since the verse goes on to say this righteousness depends on faith. Christ’s faithful obedience is the righteousness; our faith is how we receive it.

The righteousness from God. It is from God (ek theou), not from me: his own righteousness, given. And it comes through faith: faith is the channel, not the achievement. It is God’s gift, credited to believers (Romans 3:21–22; 2 Corinthians 5:21). This is what the Reformers meant by imputation: a righteousness that is not produced in me but credited to me, Christ’s record entered in my account because I am in him. Luther called it an alien righteousness: it comes from outside, and that is its comfort.

The empty hand. Faith contributes nothing; it is the empty hand. A beggar’s open palm is not what buys the bread. So assurance is possible. If my standing rested on a righteousness of my own, every bad week would move the ground under me. Because it rests on his, my standing on my worst day is exactly what it was on my best, and it will be the same on the day I am found in him. Even a believer’s best works, still mixed with sin, are accepted only because they are offered in him (1 Peter 2:5).

In the flow. Only now does verse 10 make sense: Paul wants to know Christ and share his sufferings not in order to be accepted, but because he already is. This is the gospel the Philippians are to stand firm in (1:27), and the reason the joy of 3:1 cannot be taken from them.

Where Christians differ: whose righteousness? Some interpreters, including some scholars of the New Perspective on Paul (a modern school that reads Paul’s debates as chiefly about the marks of Jewish identity), say the righteousness of my own that comes from the law means only Jewish identity, the privileges of belonging to Israel, and that the righteousness from God means God’s own covenant faithfulness, or covenant membership, rather than a righteous status credited to the believer. They rightly stress that the gospel makes Jew and Gentile one people. This commentary’s view: this verse is one of the clearest in Scripture on imputed righteousness. Paul’s list in vv. 5–6 does include his Jewish credentials, but it also includes his zeal and his blamelessness under the law, and he sets all of it against a righteousness that is God’s gift. He contrasts a righteousness of my own, from the law, with a righteousness from God, through faith. It is a status given by God, not produced by us, received by faith. This is justification by the imputed righteousness of Christ (Romans 4:5–6; the Westminster Confession 11.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1). Covenant membership follows, but the heart is a righteous standing before the Judge.

If I am clothed in Christ’s righteousness, why does my sin still matter? Because you belong to the one whose righteousness you wear. Sin no longer threatens your standing, since Christ has borne its penalty, but it grieves your Father, harms you and others, and contradicts who you now are. God disciplines his children not to pay for their sin but to make them share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). And a person who truly rests in Christ’s righteousness will want to be like him; a faith that is content to go on in sin has not understood what it was given (Romans 6:1–2). Confess your sins honestly, knowing that confession does not earn your acceptance but enjoys it.

Is it fair for God to count guilty people righteous? It would not be, if it were make-believe. A judge who simply declared a guilty man innocent would be corrupt, and Scripture says so (Proverbs 17:15). But God does not pretend. The penalty for the sins of those in Christ was really paid, at the cross, and the obedience credited to them was really lived, by Christ, every day of his life. Because believers are joined to him, his record becomes theirs as truly as their sin became his (2 Corinthians 5:21). So God is shown to be just, and also the one who justifies everyone who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Justification is not God lowering the standard. It is God meeting it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
That I may know him. Everything in the passage has been building to this. Not that I may know about him; not even that I may know his benefits. Him. The verb (ginōskō) means personal, experiential knowledge. It is the word for Adam knowing his wife, and for God’s you only have I known (Amos 3:2): the knowing that happens between persons. And the man who has seen the risen Lord and been caught up to the third heaven writes as though he were still at the beginning. Few have known Christ better, and nobody wanted to know him more.

The power of his resurrection. The power that raised Christ is at work in believers now: new life, victory over sin, strength in weakness (Ephesians 1:19–20; Romans 6:4). And the order reverses Christ’s own life, where suffering came first, because Paul describes the Christian’s experience: you meet the risen Lord first, and it is his resurrection power that then makes it possible to walk into suffering at all. Nobody shares Christ’s sufferings on his own steam.

Share his sufferings. “Share” is koinōnia, fellowship, the partnership word of chapter 1. Fellowship with Christ includes fellowship in suffering for his sake (Romans 8:17; 1 Peter 4:13). Not that our sufferings atone, but that we share his path. And Paul yokes two things we would prefer to separate: in the oldest manuscripts the power and the fellowship are held under one article, as a single object with two faces.

Becoming like him in his death. “Becoming like” is one word, symmorphizomenos, conformed to, and there is morphē again, the word from 2:6–7, the form of God and the form of a servant. The hymn is being pressed into Paul: he is being shaped into the form of the one who poured himself out. It means dying to self daily (2 Corinthians 4:10–11), and perhaps being willing to die as a martyr. The tense is continuous: a thing being done to him while he writes, in a cell, awaiting a verdict. Paul regards the suffering not as the price of the power but as part of the prize, because the person he wants to know went to a cross.

Why would anyone long for this? Most of us do not, and Paul was not asking for pain for its own sake. Five things explain his longing.

1. The goal is Christ, not the pain. The sentence begins: that I may know him. Everything after it unpacks what knowing him involves. A wife who spends nights at her husband’s hospital bed does not long for hospitals; she longs to be with him, and that is where he is. Love wants to share the beloved’s life, the hard parts too (Ruth 1:16). Paul had counted everything else as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (vv. 7–8), and he would not leave out the part of Christ’s life that was the cross.

2. In this life the power and the suffering come together. Paul names resurrection power and shared sufferings in one breath, because he had found that Christ’s power is known most deeply in weakness. My power is made perfect in weakness, the Lord told him (2 Corinthians 12:9). He carried the death of Jesus in his body so that the life of Jesus might be shown in it (2 Corinthians 4:7–11). When everyone deserted him at his trial, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). The times he suffered for Christ were the times he knew Christ nearest.

3. Suffering for Christ marks you as his. Jesus said the world would treat his followers as it treated him (John 15:18–20). So to be opposed for Christ is a sign of belonging to him. The apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). Paul tells these same Philippians that suffering for Christ has been granted to them, a gift, alongside faith (1:29).

4. The road leads to glory. Christ went through the cross to the resurrection, and his people follow the same road: becoming like him in his death, so as to attain the resurrection (v. 11). We suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). Paul weighed it and called it light, momentary affliction beside an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17; Romans 8:18).

5. Paul was in prison as he wrote. This is not a wish from a comfortable armchair. He was in chains (1:7, 13), facing possible death (1:20–23). He is not asking for a suffering he has not tasted. He is saying: I would rather have Christ with chains than comfort without him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean seeking suffering, enjoying pain, or inflicting it on yourself. Paul begged three times for his thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:8), and Jesus himself prayed that the cup might pass (Matthew 26:39). It means accepting suffering, when it comes in Christ’s service, as part of knowing him. Nor are you a poor Christian if you do not feel this longing: start by asking to know Christ, and the willingness grows as love grows.

What “dying to self” actually means. The phrase is not in the Bible, but it sums up what it says: deny yourself and take up your cross daily (Luke 9:23); I have been crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:20). It has three parts.

1. Something that has already happened. If you trust Christ, your old self, the you that was ruled by sin, was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). It is a fact you believe and then live out: consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus (Romans 6:11). Sin is no longer your master, even when it still shouts.

2. Something you do every day. The self that wants to be on the throne still fights, so each day you say no to it: my will above God’s, my comfort above another’s good, my reputation above the truth. In ordinary life: you bite back the cutting reply; you admit you were wrong, without excuses; you give up your Saturday to help someone move house; you turn down the deal that would mean bending the truth; you put to death the sins Paul names (Colossians 3:5–9).

3. Always for the sake of life. Dying to self is never the end point. The grain dies to bear much fruit (John 12:24). If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live (Romans 8:13). What dies is selfishness and sin; what lives is the real you, made new and becoming like Christ.

What dying to self does not mean.

Not erasing your personality. Paul stayed recognisably Paul: blunt, warm, learned. Your self is redeemed, not abolished.

Not self-hatred. The verse that says I have been crucified with Christ goes on: who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). You die to self as someone deeply loved, not as someone worthless.

Not being a doormat. It does not mean you may never say no, never have needs, or must let others use or abuse you. Jesus withdrew from the crowds to rest and pray (Mark 6:31). Dying to self is death to sin and selfishness, not to wisdom, boundaries or protecting the vulnerable.

Not neglecting or punishing your body. Harsh treatment of the body has no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:20–23). Rest, food, sleep and medical care are not selfishness.

Not something you manage in your own strength. It is by the Spirit that you put to death the deeds of the body (Romans 8:13).

Not the loss of joy. Whoever loses his life for Christ’s sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). The aim is not a smaller life, but a fuller one.

How do I actually get to know Christ better? The same way you come to know any person: by spending time with him and listening to him. Read the Gospels slowly, asking not only what Jesus did but what it shows you about him. Pray, and not only with requests: tell him what you are thinking and what you love about him. Come to the Lord’s Table, where he gives himself to be received by faith. Obey him, because he shows himself to those who keep his word (John 14:21). Spend time with Christians who know him well. And when hard times come in following him, do not waste them: ask to meet him there, because that is where Paul knew him nearest.

On a Tuesday. Pray Paul’s prayer this morning: Lord, let me know you, the power of your resurrection, and the fellowship of your sufferings. Then choose one ordinary way from the list above to die to self today, not to prove anything, but because you belong to the one who died for you.

verseByVerse.quote: that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That by any means possible. Literally, if somehow. Is Paul hedging about whether he will be raised, after 1:6? The letter settles it: this is the man who has said that to die is gain, and in the next verse he says Christ has already made him his own. Nobody who writes those sentences is privately unsure whether he is saved.

Open about the route. The phrase expresses not doubt about the outcome but humility about the way: whatever it takes, however God chooses to bring me there, through suffering and death if need be. Paul does not know whether he arrives by a Roman sword or an old man’s bed. He is attached not to the road but to the destination.

Certain, but not casual. A Christian can be certain of the end and still refuse to be casual about the journey: God will keep you, and you must press on. The same Paul who wrote that he who began a good work will bring it to completion also wrote, “But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27). The certainty never produces a shrug.

Attain the resurrection. “Attain” (katantaō) is to arrive at, to reach the destination. The final goal is the bodily resurrection of the righteous at Christ’s return (v. 21; 1 Corinthians 15:23). Literally it is the out-resurrection from among the dead: not merely the general raising of all, which the wicked share (John 5:28–29), but the resurrection that is glory, this humiliated body remade like Christ’s (v. 21).

Raised from the dead first. Paul’s words for his goal, resurrection from the dead, are the words the New Testament uses of Easter: Christ was raised from the dead, never to die again (Romans 6:9), the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18). Paul hopes to arrive where his Lord already is, by the road his Lord took. That is why if somehow does not shake him: the resurrection he reaches for has already happened once, to the man who met him on the Damascus road, and the resurrection of every believer is joined to that one as the harvest to its firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

Does the out-resurrection mean believers are raised at a different time from everyone else? Some read it that way, as a first resurrection of believers separated from a later one. Premillennial Christians, who expect Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years between two resurrections (Revelation 20:4–6), are faithful brothers and sisters who love the same returning Lord. But the phrase describes the character of the resurrection, not a separate timetable. Scripture teaches one return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, both the righteous and the unrighteous (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), and then the judgement: Jesus speaks of one hour in which all who are in the tombs hear his voice. For believers it is a resurrection to glory, out from among the dead and into life with Christ; for others it is a resurrection to judgement. So Paul is longing for the glorious side of that one great day, not for an earlier event.

What if I am unsure whether I will make it? Paul’s sentence is a useful corrective. Christians sometimes fear that any uncertainty in them proves their faith is counterfeit. A man utterly sure of his destination can still write a cautious-sounding line about the road, because the caution is not about God’s faithfulness but about his own ignorance of what the next year holds. Not knowing what is coming is not the same as doubting who is waiting. Your assurance rests on Christ’s promise and work, not on your ability to foresee the road (John 10:28). Keep looking to him, keep pressing on, and trust him to bring you there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Not Arrived, and Still Running
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul insists he has not yet arrived or reached perfection. He presses on to take hold of the goal because Christ has already taken hold of him. Mature believers think the same way; where they differ, God will make things clear, and meanwhile they live by what they have reached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sanctification Is Progress, Not Arrival

Holiness in this life is real but incomplete. Verse 12 is the apostle’s own testimony to that, and its order drives the Christian life: Paul presses on to lay hold of Christ because Christ has already laid hold of him.

Verse 15 adds the paradox that defines maturity: the mature are those who know they have not yet arrived.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some in the early church claimed a completed spiritual state, and Paul’s disclaimer corrects it. Where believers still differ, he hands them to God to do the persuading.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not already perfect. Having written such lofty sentences, Paul immediately puts a guard on them. “Perfect” (teleioō) means complete, mature, brought to the goal: Paul has not reached full conformity to Christ. In every century some have taught that a Christian could reach a settled plateau where the striving was over, and perhaps some in Philippi claimed it. Paul, of all people entitled to claim it, refuses.

Christ has made me his own. “Press on” (diōkō) is to pursue, to chase, and it is the word used of his persecuting the church in verse 6: the same energy, now redirected. And “make it my own” (katalambanō) is to seize, used both times. Paul is chasing Christ because Christ has already caught him. That is the logic of Christian effort in one line. He was seized on the Damascus road, travelling in the opposite direction with warrants in his bag. Grace comes first; effort follows. Running to be caught is exhausting and never finished; running because you were caught is why Paul can admit he has not arrived without the admission destroying him. The perfection he lacks has already been supplied: Christ obeyed perfectly in his place, and that obedience, not the quality of his running, is what he is found in (3:9). Every stumble in the race is real, and none of them can undo his standing.

One thing I do. Emphatic honesty, then single-minded focus. A man with a dozen churches on his conscience and a trial pending says his life has one thing in it.

Forgetting what lies behind. Biblical forgetting is not amnesia; Paul has just spent three verses listing his past. It means refusing to let it govern, whether to boast or to despair. It cuts both ways: Paul had blood on his hands and could have spent his life doing penance in his own head; and he must forget his successes, which is harder and less often preached. A man glancing back at either is losing the race.

Straining forward. “Straining forward” (epekteinomai) is stretching out toward: a runner whose chest reaches the line ahead of his legs.

The upward call. “Goal” (skopos) is the mark, the target the eye is fixed on. “Prize” (brabeion) is the victor’s wreath at the games (1 Corinthians 9:24). The upward call is God’s call to come up, perhaps as winners were called up by the herald. The prize is Christ himself, and eternal glory with him: not a trophy God hands over, but God calling his runner home.

Where Christians differ: Christian perfection. Some traditions, notably Wesleyan and Holiness churches, teach that believers can attain sinless perfection or entire sanctification, a settled state of perfect love, in this life; they rightly long for holiness and will not settle for less. This commentary’s view: the apostle Paul, late in his ministry, says he is not yet perfect and is still pressing on. Believers grow in holiness, but perfection comes only at glorification (1 John 1:8; 3:2; the Westminster Confession 13.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.2). The Christian life is a race to the end, not a plateau. Sanctification is the Spirit’s lifelong work of making a believer actually holy in heart and life; glorification is God’s finishing of that work, begun when a believer dies and goes to be with Christ and completed at the resurrection, when sin is gone for ever (Romans 8:30; Hebrews 12:23).

How do I forget what lies behind when my past is terrible, or when I was badly hurt? Forgetting does not mean pretending it did not happen, and it does not mean that wrongs done to you must never be named or brought to justice. It means that the past no longer gets to steer. If your past is your sin, it has been nailed to the cross; confess anything unconfessed, make what amends you can, and then refuse to keep paying for what Christ has paid for. If your past is what others did to you, bring it to God, get help to heal, seek justice where that is right, and ask him for the grace to forgive. Healing may take a long time. But your future is defined by the upward call of God, not by what happened behind you.

What if I feel I am barely running at all? The race is long, and runners have bad stretches. Paul’s own word for himself is that he has not arrived. What matters is the direction you are facing and that you keep getting up. Look again at the reason for the race: Christ has made you his own. Run because you are held, not to get held. Lean on other runners; the Christian race is never a solo event (Hebrews 12:1–2). And fix your eyes on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, who ran ahead of you and is waiting at the line.
verseByVerse.note: The picture is of a runner straining toward the finishing line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those of us who are mature think this way, and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you. Only let us hold true to what we have attained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are mature. The word is teleioi, and it is the same root as perfect in verse 12, where Paul denied being it. Three verses after denying he is perfect, he wryly counts himself among the mature, and that is the lesson. Maturity is not having arrived; maturity is knowing you have not.

God will reveal that also. This is a gracious sentence about disagreement. The apostle who called his opponents dogs does not press here. He hands them over to God and trusts him to correct believers on secondary matters as they grow.

Knowing which question is in front of you. On the gospel itself, whether righteousness comes by law or by faith, Paul gives no ground whatever; there the language is dogs and mutilators. On the outworking of the pressing-on life, where sincere Christians see differently, he is patient and confident that the Spirit who teaches will keep teaching. Knowing which question is in front of you is most of pastoral wisdom. Treat every disagreement as a first-order matter and you will shred a congregation; treat none of them as first-order and you will lose the gospel.

Patience, not indifference. He plainly thinks he is right, and is sure enough of the truth to let God do the persuading.

The mind that does not grasp. Think this way is phroneō, the word of 2:5, where Paul tells the church to have among themselves the mind that is theirs in Christ Jesus. The Son, who had every right to equality with God, did not grasp at it; the mature believer does not grasp at having arrived. And the promise that God will reveal is a promise about the Son. It is the Father’s delight to show his Son to those humble enough to be taught as little children (Matthew 11:25–27), and the Spirit whom Christ sent guides his people into the truth (John 16:13).

Hold true. Then the floor. “Hold true” (stoicheō) is a marching word: keep in line, walk in step with. Whatever remains unresolved, live up to the truth you already know. You do not have to solve everything before you obey anything.

How do I tell a gospel issue from a secondary one? Ask whether the question touches how a sinner is made right with God, who Christ is, or the authority of Scripture. Those are first-order: the deity and humanity of Christ, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, justification by grace through faith, the Trinity. On these, there can be no compromise. Many other matters, such as the details of church practice, views of the end times, or questions of conscience about food and days, matter and are worth discussing, but sincere believers differ on them and remain brothers. Hold your convictions firmly there too, but hold your brothers more firmly.

What should I do when I think a fellow believer is wrong on such a matter? Pray for them before you talk to them. Speak humbly, from Scripture, and listen as well as argue; you may be the one who needs correcting. Then do what Paul does: leave the persuading to God, and keep walking in step together. Do not make it a test of fellowship, do not campaign, and do not gossip. And look to your own obedience first: are you living up to what you already know?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Two Ways to Walk, and Where You Are From
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul invites them to follow his example and that of others who live the same way, because many, he says with tears, live as enemies of the cross, ruled by appetite and heading for ruin. Believers, by contrast, are citizens of heaven, waiting for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, from there. By the power with which he rules all things, he will transform their weak and humble bodies to be like his glorious body.
verseByVerse.theology:
Citizenship, and a Body That Will Be Raised

The picture in verse 20 (politeuma) is not evacuation: a Roman colony was Rome made visible on the frontier. Heavenly citizenship does not license withdrawal from the city; it tells you what you are doing there.

Verse 21 completes the pattern of the chapter 2 hymn and turns it on us. Christ took the form of a slave; the body of our humiliation will be conformed to his body of glory. The body is not the problem and will not be discarded, but changed, by the power that will subject all things to him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Join in imitating me” was said to people with no New Testament and no Christian upbringing, for whom the gospel had to be seen before it could be copied, and it was said by a man who had just admitted he had not arrived.

Now: For the one who is ill, or ageing, or watching a body they love fail, verse 21 says that what you live in now is not the last word about you.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Join in imitating me. Is that not arrogance? “Join in imitating” (symmimētai) means fellow imitators. It would be, but for three things. First, Paul always means it with the qualifier he makes explicit elsewhere: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). He is a pointing finger, not a destination. Second, these Christians had no New Testament, no shelf of books, and many were barely a decade out of paganism. The gospel had to be seen before it could be copied, and they had seen it in a man beaten with rods in their own city and singing hymns at midnight in the cell (Acts 16:22–25). Third, five verses earlier this same man wrote that he was not yet perfect. The one who says imitate me has just said he has not arrived, and that is what makes him safe to follow.

Keep your eyes on them. “Keep your eyes on” is skopeō, to watch, to mark, the same root as the goal of verse 14. And not Paul only: any life bent that way will do. Somewhere in your own congregation there is a quiet old saint worth watching more closely than you have.

Even with tears. Then Paul’s composure breaks, and that is the tone to hold on to. He is not sneering at these people or enjoying the denunciation; tears are the right posture from which to describe another person’s ruin.

Enemies of the cross. Paul does not say who they are. Probably those who professed faith while living for themselves, perhaps abusing grace as licence. He gives not a doctrinal profile but a way of walking. The cross is the pattern of chapter 2: self-emptying, obedience, the interests of others. A life organised around self-indulgence contradicts that pattern whatever it professes on a Sunday.

Their end is destruction. Four marks, and the terminus is named first, so the trajectory is visible before the symptoms. “Destruction” (apōleia) is ruin, perdition: eternal loss, the same word as 1:28. Paul does not soften it, because God is holy and does not treat sin lightly: a life that enthrones appetite ends where every rival god ends, under his judgement, shut out from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

Their god is their belly. Appetite in the place of worship: food, sex, comfort, pleasure (Romans 16:18). Whatever in you says I want has been enthroned, and it is a god that must be fed daily and never says thank you.

They glory in their shame. The boast has been inverted: the very things that should have caused them to hide are the things they advertise.

He despised the shame. Set the four marks against the cross these people are enemies of, and each one is reversed in Christ. Their end is destruction; his death rescues from destruction all who trust him. Their god is their belly; he was hungry in the wilderness and still refused to make his appetite his master (Matthew 4:2–4). They glory in their shame; he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and bore a disgrace that was ours so that his people might share his glory. Their minds are set on earthly things; his mind is the mind of 2:5, set on the Father’s will and the good of others. An enemy of the cross is the exact negative of the crucified.

Minds set on earthly things. The root of all of it. “Minds set” is phroneō, the key word of the letter again: their mindset is earthly, the opposite of the mind of Christ (2:5). It is the quietest diagnosis and the most searching. It describes not an act but an orientation: where the mind settles when nothing is demanding its attention, what you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. That is what Paul is weeping over, and it is far more ordinary than the phrase enemies of the cross leads us to expect.

In the flow. The chapter began with people who trusted the flesh by adding rules to Christ (vv. 2–3), and it ends with people who serve the flesh by indulging it. Both miss the cross from opposite directions, one by adding to it and the other by ignoring it, and Christ’s people are to follow neither.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians cannot enjoy food or earthly gifts. God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). It means those gifts must not become gods.

Can a true Christian be an enemy of the cross? A true believer can fall into serious sin for a time, as David and Peter did, and must be called to repent. But Paul is describing a settled way of life: people whose god is their appetite and whose end is destruction. Those who live that way, whatever they profess, show that they do not belong to Christ (1 John 3:6–10). That is why Paul weeps rather than shrugs. If you are troubled by this, the trouble is a good sign; enemies of the cross do not grieve over their sin. Turn to Christ now, and keep turning.

What if the people I look up to let me down? Some will, because every human model is flawed, and some who seemed strong will fall. That is why Paul points through himself to Christ. Choose models whose lives are cross-shaped, not merely gifted or successful, and watch how they handle failure as well as success. When a model falls, grieve, learn, and do not let it shake your faith in the one they were pointing to. And remember that you are someone’s model too.

verseByVerse.quote: But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But our citizenship is in heaven. “But” is the hinge: against minds set on earthly things, a fact about where his readers belong. The noun is politeuma, commonwealth, homeland, and it is the sister of the verb Paul used back in 1:27 when he told them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel. A politeuma was a body of citizens resident in a foreign place, holding the rights and duties of a homeland they might never have seen.

Living in one place, belonging to another. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with discharged legionaries and granted the standing of Italian soil, governed by Roman law. Its citizens were intensely proud of it; the charge against Paul in that very city had been that he was advocating customs “not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice” (Acts 16:21). Paul takes the proudest fact about their city as a picture of something truer: your capital is not Rome. The church is a colony of heaven on earth.

Not evacuation. Citizenship in heaven is not a promise of evacuation or permission to disengage. A Roman colony was not homesick expatriates waiting for a boat; it was Rome visible on the frontier. Paul is telling them what they are doing in Philippi.

We await a Saviour. The verb (apekdechomai) is a strong compound: to await eagerly, expectantly, as in Romans 8:19–25. Sōtēr, saviour, and kyrios, lord, were both claimed by Caesar; the emperor was hailed as saviour and lord. In a colony of Caesar’s veterans, Paul says quietly that the Saviour and Lord is someone else.

The Lord Jesus Christ. He will come from heaven, as an emperor might visit a colony to rescue it. The question is not whether you believe he is coming, but whether anything in the way you live this week would only make sense if he were.

Should Christians care about their country, vote or serve in public life? Yes, but as citizens of heaven first. Paul used his Roman citizenship when it served the gospel (Acts 16:37; 22:25), and he told Christians to pray for those in authority and to seek the good of their society (1 Timothy 2:1–2; Romans 13:1–7). Love your neighbour, work for justice, vote with a conscience shaped by Scripture, and serve where you are called. But do not put your ultimate hope in any party, leader or nation, and do not let earthly loyalties outrank Christ. When the two conflict, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Will we live in heaven for ever? Our citizenship is in heaven now, and believers who die go to be with Christ there (1:23). But the final hope is not a disembodied existence. Christ will come from heaven, raise the dead, and make all things new: a new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–4). The capital comes down to the colony. God will dwell with his people, in resurrected bodies, in a renewed creation, for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Philippi’s citizens were proud to be citizens of Rome; believers belong to a heavenly commonwealth.

verseByVerse.quote: who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our lowly body. The hymn of chapter 2 is turned on us: as Christ was humbled and exalted, so he will transform our lowly body. “Transform” (metaschēmatizō) is to change the form, the outward state. “Our lowly body” is literally the body of our humiliation, and the word is the noun from the same root as he humbled himself in 2:8. Paul is naming what everyone over forty knows: these bodies are weak, ageing, sick and dying (2 Corinthians 4:16; 5:4), and anyone who has watched a strong parent become unable to manage a staircase knows he has not exaggerated.

Like his glorious body. “Like” is symmorphos, conformed, and it is built on morphē again, the same root as the form of God in 2:6 and becoming like him in his death in verse 10. The pattern completes: he took our form so that we might share his. The resurrection body will be like Christ’s risen body: imperishable, glorious, powerful (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; 1 John 3:2).

Transformation, not escape. Much Greek thought around Philippi held that salvation meant the soul getting free of the body. Paul says it will be changed: the same body, made glorious, as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his own, still bearing the marks of the nails (John 20:27), and yet transfigured. So the body is not to be worshipped, nor despised: it has a glorious future.

The power to subject all things. Then the guarantee: the same power by which Christ will rule all creation (Psalm 8:6; 1 Corinthians 15:27). The energy that will bring the whole created order under Christ’s feet, death included, will be applied to your body.

Where the chapter has been going. Paul opened by throwing his pedigree out with the kitchen refuse and closes with the humiliated body made glorious. That is why minds must not be set on earthly things: not because earthly things are unreal, but because they are not where the story is going.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become divine. We will be glorified humans, like Christ in his humanity, never sharing his deity.

What about bodies that were destroyed, cremated or lost at sea? The resurrection does not depend on the condition of the remains. The God who made the first body from the dust can raise it from any dust. The power that subjects all things to Christ is not limited by fire, sea or decay (Revelation 20:13). Christians may differ on burial and cremation as a matter of practice and witness, but no believer’s resurrection is in any doubt because of how their body was laid to rest.

What does this mean for someone who is disabled, ill or ageing? It means your present weakness is not the last word about you. The body of humiliation will be raised in power and glory, free from pain, disease and decay. Every limitation sin brought into the world will be undone. That does not make present suffering small, and you are free to grieve it and to seek every help now. But you may also hope, concretely and bodily. Many disabled believers have said that the first face they will see with perfect eyes, and the first steps they take on perfect legs, will be towards Christ. The New Testament does not tell you the body does not matter. It tells you the body matters so much that God intends to raise it.

For worship. Christ wore the body of humiliation before we did. He was weary at a well, wept at a grave, was scourged and crucified and laid in another man’s tomb, and on the third day that same body came out glorious. He did not leave our frailty behind when he rose; he carried our nature up into glory, and from the throne he will reach down with the power that rules all things and lift every one of his people out of the dust. The aged, the broken and the buried will rise in his likeness, and the eyes that closed in death will open on his face.
