4.title: The Peace That Passes Understanding: Rejoice, Pray, and Be Content
4.overview:
The last chapter gathers the letter’s threads into practice. First, a quarrel: two women who had worked hard beside Paul have fallen out, and he pleads with them by name to agree in the Lord. Then a cluster of commands for a church under strain: joy, gentleness, prayer in place of anxiety, a mind filled with what is good, and a life that practises what it has learned.

Finally Paul thanks them, delicately, for the gift Epaphroditus carried. He is grateful, but he has learned contentment in plenty and in want through Christ who strengthens him, and he closes with praise, greetings and grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Stand Firm, and Two Women Who Cannot Agree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul calls the church he loves to hold their ground in the Lord, then names a painful problem inside it: two of his co-workers have fallen out, and he asks a trusted colleague to help them make peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Christian Unity Rests On

The appeal to these two women shows the ground of unity: not agreement on every point but a shared life in Christ, one Lord, one Spirit, one book of life. A congregation whose unity rests on consensus will fracture at the first serious disagreement; one whose unity rests on Christ can carry real friction without breaking.

Paul does not adjudicate or pull rank, and he ends not with a warning but with election: their names are written in heaven, and that is the deeper fact about them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: These were not marginal figures. The Philippian church had begun among women at a riverside prayer meeting (Acts 16:13), so they had very likely been in it from the first day.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, my beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Philippians 4 gathers the letter’s joy, unity and partnership into practical exhortation and warm thanks: a plea to two quarrelling fellow workers (vv. 1–3), some of the best-loved commands in Scripture (vv. 4–9), and thanks for a gift, with the secret of contentment and the promise that God will supply every need (vv. 10–23).

Therefore. The word reaches back to 3:20–21: our citizenship is in heaven, and Christ will transform our bodies by the power that subjects all things to himself. Therefore stand firm. The command to hold the line is not a demand for grit. It rests on a promise about how the story ends.

Whom I love and long for. Six endearments in a single verse, and two of them are the same Greek word, one near each end, so that the command sits inside affection like a stone in a fist of wool. Paul is about to name two women in a public letter, and he builds the setting first. “Long for” picks up the ache of 1:8, where he yearned for them with the affection of Christ.

My joy and crown. “Crown” is stephanos: not the royal diadem but the victor’s wreath at the games. The runner of 3:14 tells this congregation that they are the wreath, the evidence on the last day that his labour was not in vain (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20). People are the prize.

Stand firm thus. “Stand firm” is the word of 1:27, the picture of a line that holds when it is pushed. The little word thus gathers the letter: stand firm like that, as citizens of heaven, in the Christ who has laid hold of you (3:12, 20).

The ground already taken. The ground under the line is Christ himself. He stood firm when every friend fled (Mark 14:50), did not turn back from the cross, and has already won the field. The believer does not stand in his own resolve but in a Lord whose victory is finished, and his people hold because he holds them (John 10:28).

The seam inside. The command to hold the line comes straight before the naming of a quarrel: for Paul they are the same subject. A congregation does not usually break because a persecutor smashes it from outside; it breaks along a seam that opened inside it.

What does standing firm look like in an ordinary week? It looks less like heroism and more like staying put. Keep meeting with your church when you are tired or disappointed. Keep holding to the gospel when you hear clever voices that would add to it or take from it (3:2). Keep obeying in the area where temptation presses hardest. Keep loving the believers next to you in the line, especially the difficult ones. And do it in the Lord: by praying, by remembering what he has promised, and by leaning on the people beside you. A line holds because each person stays where he is and trusts the one next to him.
verseByVerse.note: The “crown” is the victor’s wreath awarded at the games.

verseByVerse.quote: I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord. Yes, I ask you also, true companion, help these women, who have labored side by side with me in the gospel together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Euodia and Syntyche. One of the very few New Testament quarrels reported with the parties named, serious enough to reach Paul in prison (2:1–4). He does something so exposing gently: he does not say who is right, or what the dispute was about, or invoke his authority. The verb, I appeal, comes twice, once for each woman, so as not to take sides. No one hearing the letter read aloud could tell which of them Paul thought had started it.

To agree in the Lord. Literally, to think the same thing (to auto phronein) in the Lord, and it is the exact phrase from 2:2 and the mind of 2:5. He is not asking for the same conclusion but the same mind, which is Christ’s, and that mind is described in the hymn: not grasping, counting the other more significant. The ground of reunion is not the settling of the argument. It is a Lord they both already have.

True companion. Then he brings in a third party, which churches are notoriously bad at. The true companion is unnamed. The word is syzygos, yokefellow, one of a pair of oxen pulling together, and it may even be a man’s name, Syzygus, with Paul punning that he is true to it. Most quarrels are left to sort themselves out and therefore harden. Paul assigns this one to a trusted person, in a letter everyone will hear.

Help these women. Before anyone can think of these two as troublemakers, he tells the church who they are. “Laboured side by side” (synathleō) is the athletic word of 1:27, contending together like a team. These were front-rank gospel workers. The Philippian church began among women at a riverside, with Lydia (Acts 16:13–15).

The book of life. That is where Paul leaves them. The book of life is God’s register of his people, the citizens of heaven (Daniel 12:1; Luke 10:20). Their names are written there: they are God’s elect, chosen before the world began for salvation in Christ, not because of their works but because of his own purpose and grace (Ephesians 1:4–5; 2 Timothy 1:9). Their quarrel is real, but it is not the truest thing about them. That is how a church should learn to see the people who exasperate it: the disagreement is a fact, but their names in heaven are a deeper fact.

The Lamb’s book. Revelation gives the register its full name: the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8; 21:27). The names are not there because the people were impressive, and they do not stay there because the people behave well. They are there because the Lamb was slain for them. That is the deepest reason Euodia and Syntyche must be reconciled. Christ did not die to prove one of them right and the other wrong; he died for both. A quarrel between two people he bought at the same price is a quarrel he has already paid to end.

Where Christians differ: can names be erased from the book of life? Some read Revelation 3:5 and Exodus 32:33 as showing that names once written can be blotted out, so believers may be lost; many earnest Christians hold this out of a proper respect for Scripture’s warnings. This commentary’s view: the book of life records those chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 17:8). Christ promises that he will never blot out the names of those who overcome (Revelation 3:5), and all true believers overcome (1 John 5:4). The names of God’s elect are written permanently. This is the security in which Paul can speak of his fellow workers.

What does this say about women’s ministry? Paul honours these women as fellow workers who laboured side by side with him in the gospel; their work was real and valued. He does not say what it was, and nothing here suggests they were elders or preached in the church’s gathering, which Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:2). This commentary holds that reading because Paul grounds it in creation rather than in local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), while gladly recognising that many faithful Christians understand those verses differently. Women served the gospel in many ways in Paul’s churches, in hospitality, teaching other women and children, supporting the mission and speaking of Christ, and they still should. A church that does not value and thank its women workers as Paul did has not understood him.

I am at odds with someone in my church. Should others be involved? Begin privately. Go to the person yourself, humbly, owning your part first, and try to be reconciled (Matthew 5:23–24; 18:15). If that fails, ask one or two wise, trusted believers to help, as Paul asked his true companion: not to take sides, but to help you both think the same thing in the Lord. Avoid recruiting supporters, which only hardens a quarrel into a faction. Paul named Euodia and Syntyche because their quarrel was already public and affecting the church. Most disagreements can and should be healed long before they reach that stage.

How would I know whether my name is written in heaven? Not by trying to read heaven’s register, but by looking to Christ. Everyone who trusts him as Lord and Saviour has been chosen in him (Ephesians 1:4), and Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20). If you are trusting Christ, your name is there, written before the foundation of the world. And the evidence grows as you follow him: love for his people, desire to obey, grief over sin. If you are not yet trusting him, the invitation is open today.
verseByVerse.note: The “true companion” is unnamed; some suggest Luke or Epaphroditus. The book of life is God’s register of his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Rejoice, Do Not Be Anxious, and Mind What You Dwell On
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A run of short commands for a church under strain, each resting on the nearness of the Lord: joy in him, gentleness to all, prayer in place of anxiety, a mind filled with what is good, and a life that practises what it learned. The run ends with the God of peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Anxiety and Its Remedy

Verses 6 and 7 are the New Testament’s most direct treatment of anxiety, and the structure of the sentence is the argument: not anything, but in everything, the same scope on both sides. Each item is moved, one by one, from worry into prayer, with thanksgiving.

Not change, nor the request granted, but peace is promised, arriving while the trouble is still sitting there. In a garrison town like Philippi the picture was plain: a garrison does not remove the threat; it stands between the threat and the people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philippians had ample material for anxiety: their apostle facing a capital charge, a quarrel inside the church, opposition outside it, and a future nobody could see. Paul offers not resolution but a practice and a promise, in the middle of the unresolved.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice. Let your reasonableness be known to everyone. The Lord is at hand;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice always. Having said at 3:1 that he does not mind repeating himself, he repeats himself inside a single verse: a man under a capital charge, writing to a church with a quarrel in it, doubles the word joy. It is repeated because it is hard to believe and easy to forget.

In the Lord. Always is only possible because of in the Lord. Joy attached to circumstances can never be always, since circumstances are not always. Joy whose object is a Lord who never changes can be commanded without cruelty (see 3:1).

Reasonableness. The word is epieikes: gentleness, forbearance, sweet reasonableness. Aristotle used it of the judge who knows when the strict letter of the law would do an injustice. It is the quality of the person who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed, and it is the quality Christ showed: Paul appeals to the Corinthians by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1).

The mind of chapter 2 in social clothing. Christ had every right and did not grasp; the gentle man has a case and does not press it to the wall. Such gentleness is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22–23), Christ’s own meekness grown in his people. And it is to be known to everyone: the neighbours, the magistrates, the pagan household next door. Paul is describing the reputation a Christian community should have in a town: not that they are right, but that they are not grasping.

The Lord is at hand. Two senses at once. Near in time: his return is coming (3:20; James 5:8), which is why you can let an injustice stand unavenged. If the Judge is on the road, you are free to stop prosecuting your own case. Near in presence: he is close to his people (Psalm 145:18), at your elbow, which is why you need not fight for your own corner. It is also the bridge to what follows: since the Lord is near, do not be anxious.

In the flow. The commands of verses 4–9 follow straight on from the quarrel: they are the climate in which two estranged sisters can be reconciled. The run ends with the God of peace (v. 9), and peace is exactly what Euodia and Syntyche had lost.

Does this mean a Christian may not grieve, or must hide depression? No. Jesus wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35), Paul tells us to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), and he says we grieve, though not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Joy in the Lord is not a cheerful mood; it can sit beside tears, under them, as the settled knowledge that Christ is ours. A believer in depression has not failed this command. He may hold on to the Lord, sometimes with nothing left but a thread, and the joy is his even when he cannot feel it.

How can I be gentle when I am in the right? By remembering that being right does not require winning. Gentleness is not weakness or silence about truth; Paul has just called false teachers dogs. It is the refusal to press every claim, prove every point and repay every slight. Speak the truth, but in a tone that leaves the other person room. Let small wrongs go. Ask whether insisting on your rights will help the other person or only satisfy you. And remember who is near: the Lord sees, and he will put right what needs putting right. You do not have to.

verseByVerse.quote: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not anything, but in everything. The first clause alone would be unbearable: nobody has stopped worrying by trying. But the sentence is a swap. Every single thing you were going to be anxious about is to be moved, item by item, into prayer. Paul is not suppressing the worry; he is redirecting it. The word is the one Jesus uses in Matthew 6:25–34 and to Martha (Luke 10:41), the mind pulled in many directions at once. Anxiety does not usually feel like fear; it feels like being unable to settle.

Prayer and supplication. Prayer is the general word. Supplication is the specific one: asking for a definite thing. That matters, because vague prayer relieves nothing; the thing keeping you awake is never vague.

With thanksgiving. This changes the whole transaction: thanks for past mercies, and in advance for his answer, whatever it is. It is what keeps petition from becoming a list of grievances read aloud to God. You cannot at the same moment thank him for what he has done and accuse him of not caring.

Made known to God. He knows them already, of course (Matthew 6:8). The making known is not for his information; it is the act of handing over, and it has to be done in words, because that is how a creature lets go of something. Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Peter 5:7). And it touches something deeper than nerves. Much anxiety is the heart trying to hold what only God can hold: the future, other people, the outcome. Handing it over in words is a confession that he is God and we are not, which is why it brings rest.

The peace of God. Paul does not say the circumstances will change, or that the request will be granted, or that you will understand why. He says peace will come. Not only peace with God, which believers have through justification (Romans 5:1), but God’s own peace, the calm that belongs to him, given to us. It surpasses understanding because it is not the peace of a resolved problem, but peace while the problem sits there unresolved. God keeps in perfect peace the one whose mind is stayed on him, because he trusts in him (Isaiah 26:3).

Will guard. The verb is a soldier’s word: to garrison, to mount guard over a city. Anyone in Philippi, a colony settled by Roman veterans, knew what that meant: a garrison does not remove the threat; it stands between the threat and the people. God’s peace does not evict every danger from the world. It stands sentry over heart and mind, the feelings and the thoughts, the two doors anxiety comes in by, and holds the gate.

In Christ Jesus. The peace that guards believers is not a technique; it is the peace of a person. On the night before he died, with the cross a few hours away, Jesus said to his frightened disciples, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you,” and told them not to let their hearts be troubled (John 14:27). And the one to whom we bring our requests is a high priest who has felt what we feel, so that we may draw near with confidence and find grace to help in time of need (Hebrews 4:15–16). Anxious hearts are kept in him.

Where Christians differ: is anxiety always sin? Some teach that any anxiety shows lack of faith; others dismiss this command as unrealistic. This commentary’s view: Paul commands believers not to be ruled by anxiety, and gives the remedy: prayer with thanksgiving. Feeling anxious is part of life in a fallen world, and even Jesus was troubled (John 12:27). Paul uses the same word of his own anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28), and of Timothy’s genuine concern (2:20). The sin is not in feeling, but in refusing to bring our fears to God and trust him: the worry we nurse rather than bring. Some anxiety has physical causes, and many believers suffer from anxiety disorders as real as any other illness. Using medical help, a doctor or counsellor, and medication where it is wise, is not a failure of faith, any more than Paul’s advice to Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). But for every anxious believer, prayer and God’s promised peace are the first and deepest help: bring it to God, again and again, and let his peace guard you while any treatment does its work.

I prayed, and I still feel anxious. What now? Pray again. Paul does not say do this once. The command is continuous, and many believers find they must hand the same burden over many times a day, especially at first. Make the prayer specific, name the fear, and add thanks for specific mercies. Then turn to what you can do: the next practical step, and the thoughts of verse 8. Tell a trusted Christian, so that you are not carrying it alone. The peace may come gradually, or as a quiet steadiness rather than a feeling of calm. Its absence for a time does not mean God has not heard; Jesus himself prayed in anguish in Gethsemane before he rose and went to the cross in peace.

Is it right to pray about small things? Yes. In everything means everything: a lost key, a hard conversation, a child’s exam, a sore back. If it is big enough to worry about, it is big enough to pray about. Nothing is too small for a Father who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30), and praying about small things is often how we learn to trust him with large ones.

On a Tuesday. Write down what is making you anxious today, item by item, and beside each one write one thing you can thank God for. Bring each to him by name. Then put the list away and get on with the day.
verseByVerse.note: “Guard” is a military word, fitting a city with a Roman garrison.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever is true. Having garrisoned the mind, Paul now says what to put in it, and much of the list is not distinctively Christian vocabulary at all. True stands at the head: real, honest, in line with God’s truth, not illusion, flattery or slander.

Honourable, just, pure, lovely. Honourable is dignified, worthy of respect, not trivial or crude. Just is what conforms to God’s standard. Pure is morally clean, not polluted by lust. Lovely is winsome, what draws out love; commendable is of good report.

Any excellence. “Excellence” is aretē, virtue, the great word of Greek moral philosophy, and Paul uses it only here. He picks up the language a thoughtful pagan would have used about the good life and hands it to the church. He is not endorsing a morality that has no need of God; he has just called certain teachers dogs (3:2). He is saying that wherever something genuinely true or lovely or admirable turns up, in a pagan poet, a piece of music, an honest neighbour, a well-made thing, it is a fragment of the goodness of the God who made the world, and a Christian is entitled to dwell on it.

Think about these things. The verb is the accountant’s: reckon. It is deliberate mental bookkeeping, not daydreaming.

Inside the walls. The peace of God garrisons the mind; verse 8 is what you do inside the walls. A guarded mind still has to be furnished, and if you do not choose the furniture, something else will. The honest test is not what you would list as your interests but what your mind reaches for when it is tired: what you scroll to, replay, rehearse. That is your actual diet.

The list has a face. Paul does not name Christ in this verse, but every word on the list has already been worn by him. He is the truth (John 14:6). He is the Holy and Righteous One whom Jerusalem denied (Acts 3:14). He alone is worthy of all praise (Revelation 5:12). All things were made through him and hold together in him (Colossians 1:16–17), so every true and lovely thing in the world is something of his. A Christian who dwells on these things is being drawn toward the one in whom they are whole.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring evil. Whatever is true heads the list, and much that is true is grim: this letter contains a prison, a near-fatal illness and a quarrel. The list is a test of what is worth dwelling on, and the difference between facing something and marinating in it is the whole distance between wisdom and morbidity. Nor does it mean only explicitly Christian things are good: whatever is true and excellent, wherever found, belongs to God (what theologians call common grace: his goodness to all people, believers or not).

Can I watch films or read books that portray sin? The Bible itself portrays sin honestly, from Cain to Judas, and it does so truthfully: sin is shown as sin, and its end is shown. So the question is not whether a story contains evil but how it treats it, and what it does to you. Does it tell the truth about good and evil, or make wickedness attractive? Does it inflame lust, harden you to cruelty or make you cynical? Would you be glad to have Christ beside you watching it? Consciences differ on details (Romans 14:5), but this verse gives the test. Choose what helps you think about what is true, honourable and pure, and be ruthless with what pulls you the other way, especially with anything that feeds lust (Matthew 5:29).

How do I stop dwelling on thoughts I do not want? You cannot usually empty your mind by force; you can only fill it with something better. When an unwanted thought comes, whether a temptation, a grievance or a fear, do not argue with it endlessly. Turn it into a prayer, then deliberately turn your attention to something on Paul’s list: a psalm, a promise, a good memory, a useful task, a conversation with a friend. Guard what goes in, because what you feed grows. And if intrusive, distressing thoughts persist despite your efforts, that may be a matter for medical help as well as prayer; it is not necessarily a sign of spiritual failure.

On a Tuesday. God’s peace already stands guard over your mind in Christ (v. 7), so furnish it gladly: run what you read, watch and scroll through today past Paul’s list, remove one thing that fails it, and add one that passes: a chapter of Scripture, a good book, a piece of music, a walk where you notice what God has made.

verseByVerse.quote: What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me—practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Learned and received. Verse 8 was about thinking; verse 9 is about doing. The four verbs fall into two pairs. Learned and received are the words for teaching handed over: “received” is the word for receiving authoritative tradition (1 Corinthians 15:1, 3).

Heard and seen in me. Heard and seen are different: they had listened to Paul and watched him live, in their own town. Doctrine and demonstration: the message and the man (3:17). They had no New Testament, only apostolic teaching and an apostle they had seen beaten in their marketplace (Acts 16:22–25). It remains true that most people learn Christianity from a Christian before they learn it from a book. Somebody is currently learning it from you, whether or not you would have volunteered for the job.

Behind the apostle, Christ. What the Philippians learned and watched was not finally Paul. The teaching was about Christ: Paul received his gospel through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12), and passed on what he had received, that Christ died for our sins and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The life was a copy of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), a servant walking the path of the Master. Christianity has always been passed on in this double way, because it began with a Word made flesh, heard and seen and touched (1 John 1:1). Doctrine and life belong together because in Christ they were never apart.

Practice these things. The verb is continuous: keep on doing. Not admire them: do them. And no one does them perfectly, Paul included (3:12). Christ alone obeyed in full, and his obedience is counted as ours (3:9; Romans 5:19), so our halting practice is accepted for his sake, and a failure does not undo our standing.

And the God of peace will be with you. The promise differs from verse 7. There, prayer brought the peace of God. Here obedience brings the God of peace himself, present with them. Paul has moved from the gift to the Giver, which is what the anxious heart was actually short of all along.

The God who makes peace. Paul reaches for this title where relationships are in question (Romans 16:20). It means the God who makes peace, who made it between himself and rebels at the cross, and who is therefore entirely capable of making it between two women in Macedonia who have stopped speaking. Seven verses after Euodia and Syntyche, that is not an accident.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s presence is earned by obedience. The letter has already ruled that out: God is at work in them to will and to work (2:13), and it is he who will complete what he began (1:6). It means those who walk in his ways enjoy his fellowship (John 14:21, 23). A disobedient believer is not abandoned, only in no condition to feel the company he is in. Obedience does not purchase the presence. It clears the window.

I have no Paul to watch. Who do I learn from? You have Paul in his letters, and Christ himself in the Gospels, and that is the first place to look. But God also gives living examples. Look in your own church for believers whose lives match their words, often older and less visible than the ones on the platform, and spend time with them: in their homes, at work alongside them, in prayer. Read the lives of faithful Christians from the past. And remember that you are learning not only from the gifted but from the faithful. The Philippians learned as much from Paul in the stocks as from Paul in the pulpit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–23 — The Secret of Contentment, and the Last Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks them for their renewed gift, carefully: he is glad of it, but his contentment never depended on it. He recalls their partnership from the first days, calls the gift a sacrifice that pleases God, promises that God will meet their needs in Christ, and closes with praise, greetings and grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Contentment Is Learned, Not Issued

Paul borrows the Stoics’ own term for self-sufficiency, the wise man who needs nothing outside himself, and reverses its content: his sufficiency is not in himself at all but in a person who keeps supplying him.

Two verses here are often misused, and both are better than their misuse. The all things of verse 13 are hunger and plenty, being brought low and abounding: not a promise that Christ will help you succeed, but that he will hold you steady in any conditions, which is worth far more. And verse 19 says need, not want, and promises a supply scaled to God’s riches rather than merely drawn from them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi was the standing exception to Paul’s usual practice. He normally refused money from the churches he worked among (1 Corinthians 9:14–18), but let these support him: a poor congregation that gave beyond its means and begged for the privilege (2 Corinthians 8:1–5), and that began sending help within weeks of his leaving their city.

Now: Paul thanks warmly, without a rebuke for the delay, and says plainly that he is well supplied, so that a poor church does not strip itself further. And God’s supply in verse 19 had just come through a church that sent a man far with a gift: the promise is usually kept through somebody, which makes it a job to take up as well as a comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoiced in the Lord greatly that now at length you have revived your concern for me. You were indeed concerned for me, but you had no opportunity. Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I rejoiced in the Lord. Now the thank-you. Paul has held it back so that nobody can suppose his joy depended on the money, and even his gratitude is in the Lord: he sees God behind their generosity.

Revived your concern. The verb is a gardener’s word: to bloom again, to put out fresh shoots, like a plant in spring. They did not wake up; they blossomed. Their care had been there all along, like a root under frozen ground, and the season finally turned.

No opportunity. One of the kindest sentences in the letter. Perhaps they had no messenger, or no money; Paul will not let his gratitude imply a rebuke for the delay. Most of us thank people in ways that quietly bill them for the wait.

Not that I am speaking of being in need. He is not hinting for more, and he does not want them to think the apostle’s wellbeing rests on their remittances.

I have learned. Contentment was not part of Paul’s temperament: read his letters and you meet a driven, intense, combative man. Nor did it arrive with his conversion. It was learned, which means there were lessons, and a period of not yet knowing. Contentment is not a gift given only to placid people.

Content. The word is autarkēs, self-sufficient, and Paul has borrowed it from the Stoics, for whom it described the wise man who needs nothing outside himself and is therefore untouchable. Paul keeps the word and reverses its content.

My grace is sufficient. Paul’s sufficiency does not come from himself but from Christ. When he begged to be rid of his thorn, the Lord Jesus answered, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9), using the same root as Paul’s word for content. Paul is content not because he needs nothing, but because the one he needs never fails, and Christ’s grace has proved sufficient in every cell Paul has sat in. Stoic contentment shrinks the heart until nothing can hurt it; Christian contentment fills it with Christ until nothing can rob it.

In the flow. Paul closes the frame he opened at 1:5, their partnership in the gospel, with thanks for its latest gift, brought by Epaphroditus (2:25–30).

Is it wrong to want a better job, house or situation? No. Paul tells slaves who can gain their freedom to take it (1 Corinthians 7:21, on the most likely reading), and he himself hoped for release from prison. Working, planning and praying for a better situation is not discontent. Discontent is when your peace and joy depend on getting it: when you cannot be thankful now, cannot rest in God now, and resent him for what you lack. Content people may still pursue change, but they do it with open hands, and they are not undone if the answer is no.

How do I thank people well? Learn from Paul. Thank God first, so that the gift points you to him. Then thank the giver specifically, warmly and soon. Do not add a sting, such as a complaint about the delay or the size. If there were obstacles, acknowledge them generously. Do not hint for more. And tell them what their gift has done, as Paul does in verse 18. Gratitude expressed well is itself a gift to the giver.

verseByVerse.quote: I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In any and every circumstance, I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brought low, and abound. Both halves are skills. “Brought low” is the very word used of Christ who humbled himself (2:8). Poverty tempts to despair or envy; plenty tempts to pride and forgetting God: give me neither poverty nor riches, lest I be full and deny you (Proverbs 30:8–9). Plenty has ruined at least as many Christians as poverty.

I have learned the secret. One Greek word, the technical term for initiation into the mystery cults. Paul is lightly ironic: here is the initiation, hunger and plenty. The secret is not whispered in a candlelit room; it is learned in the circumstances themselves.

I can do all things. Perhaps the most misquoted sentence in the Bible, printed on sports gear. In context the all things are hunger and plenty: Christ will hold him steady through any conditions whatever.

Him who strengthens me. “Strengthens” means to put power into, and the tense is continuous and personal: the one who keeps on pouring strength into me. A supply line, open now: the supply Paul counted on in 1:19, the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ: Christ strengthens his people through his Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16), the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 8:11). What does that strength look like? Usually not a surge of feeling, but the ability to do the next right thing without bitterness: to keep praying, to keep loving, to say thank you from a cell. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16).

Where Christians differ: what does “all things” mean? This verse is often quoted to mean that Christ will help believers achieve any goal: win a game, pass an exam, succeed in business. This commentary’s view: in context, all things means all circumstances: Paul can endure hunger as well as plenty, imprisonment as well as freedom, because Christ strengthens him. It is a verse about contentment and endurance in God’s will, not about achieving our ambitions. Christ does give strength for every task he assigns, but the promise is to do his will, not ours.

A promotion, not a demotion. A promise that Christ will help you win is worth little, because most of life is not winnable and one day you will lose everything you have. A promise that Christ will make you sufficient in any circumstance, including those with no way out, is worth having on the worst day of your life. The verse is for the man in the cell, which is where it was written.

What if I feel I cannot cope at all? Then you are in exactly the place where this verse begins to work. Paul does not say I can do all things because I am strong. He says through him who strengthens me, and Christ’s strength is made perfect in weakness. Tell him honestly that you cannot cope. Ask for strength for today only, not for the whole road (Matthew 6:34). Accept help from others, because Christ often strengthens us through his people, as he strengthened Paul through Epaphroditus. Do the next small thing. And if you are overwhelmed for a long time, seek practical and medical help too. Being at the end of your strength is not failure. It is where his begins.

On a Tuesday. Ask which test you are in at the moment: being brought low, or abounding. If it is want, ask Christ for strength to be content and not bitter. If it is plenty, ask him for strength not to forget him, and give something away this week, glad that your heart is not held by it.

For worship. Christ is enough. He knew both want and plenty himself: he had nowhere to lay his head, and he owned the cattle on a thousand hills. He pours his strength into weak servants day by day, and the supply has never once run dry. The secret of contentment is not a technique. It is a person, and he is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet it was kind of you to share my trouble. And you Philippians yourselves know that in the beginning of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving, except you only. Even in Thessalonica you sent me help for my needs once and again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Share my trouble. Having explained that he did not need the gift, Paul makes sure they know he is glad of it. The verb carries the partnership root of 1:5: to become partners in. They did not send money to a distant cause; they got into the trouble with him.

The beginning of the gospel. This means the early days of his mission in Europe, about ten years before, and his precision shows how much he has kept count.

Except you only. Giving and receiving is the language of a ledger with two columns, a shared account: they gave material help; he gave spiritual blessing (Romans 15:27). In the earliest days, when the mission was unproven, exactly one church backed him with money: not Jerusalem, not Antioch, but a small assembly in a Roman colony, one of the Macedonian churches which, Paul told the Corinthians, gave out of extreme poverty, beyond their means, and begged for the privilege (2 Corinthians 8:1–5).

Even in Thessalonica. Thessalonica was Paul’s next stop after Philippi (Acts 17:1), about a hundred miles down the Egnatian Way. So the Philippians supported him almost the moment he walked out of their gates, more than once, while their church was weeks old.

The standing exception. He generally refused money from the churches he was working among, supporting himself by his trade so that no one could say he preached for pay (1 Corinthians 9:14–18; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9). Philippi was the standing exception. This poor, new, frightened church worked out at once what many established congregations never do: that the gospel travels on somebody’s money, and that they had better be the somebody.

Grace in Macedonia. Holding up these churches to the Corinthians, Paul called their giving the grace of God given among them (2 Corinthians 8:1), and within a few sentences he traced it to its source: the Lord Jesus Christ, rich beyond measure, made himself poor so that others might be made rich by his poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9). A poor church gave beyond its means because it had been given to beyond all measure.

Should pastors and missionaries be paid? Yes, as a rule. The Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and the worker deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18). Paul gave up that right in some places for the sake of the gospel, but he never said it was wrong to receive support. A church that supports its pastor and sends money to missionaries is not doing them a favour; it is entering into partnership, as the Philippians did. It is also right to give in ways that do not create dependence or obligation that would hinder the work.

How do I decide what to give? Give regularly, proportionately and cheerfully. On the first day of every week, Paul told the Corinthians, each should put something aside as he may prosper (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give as you have decided in your heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Begin with your local church, which feeds you, and include gospel work further afield. Many Christians take a tenth as a starting point and grow from there. The Philippians are the model: they gave early, gave often and gave beyond their means, and Paul remembered it with joy.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had gone on from Philippi to Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit that increases to your credit. I have received full payment, and more. I am well supplied, having received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent, a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit that increases to your credit. Paul turns the accounting metaphor round: he is after what the giving is doing in the givers. “Credit” is an account, and increases is the word for interest accruing. His concern is not that the mission is short of funds, but that a Christian who gives is being changed by it, and one who does not is missing something that would have done him good. It is what Jesus meant by treasure in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy (Matthew 6:19–21).

Full payment. The word was written on receipts in the ancient world: paid in full. Paul’s receipt is quietly protective: to a congregation in extreme poverty, it says, that is sufficient, do not strip yourselves further. Gratitude that does not know how to say enough can bleed generous people dry.

A fragrant offering. Then the ledger becomes an altar. This is Old Testament sacrifice language (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9), the smell of a sacrifice rising and being received. A gift carried hundreds of miles by a man who nearly died in the work (2:27, 30), and Paul says: that was worship. It went up (Hebrews 13:16).

The fragrance of Christ. Paul uses the phrase of Christ, who loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2). That is why a gift of money can rise to God at all. Believers offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5): their gifts smell sweet because they are offered by people who are in him, and each one is a small copy of his self-giving. The Philippians gave themselves away for Paul because Christ had first given himself away for them.

Re-routed. They sent it to Paul; God received it. So ordinary practical help, a meal, a lift, a spare room, is not the poor relation of worship. It is the same act, and God is the one who smells the smoke.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving earns salvation. It is an offering of thanks from those already saved, and God graciously rewards it.

Is it wrong to give hoping for a reward? Not if the reward is the one God promises. Jesus himself said to lay up treasure in heaven, and that the Father who sees in secret will reward (Matthew 6:4). But the reward is not a better return on your money in this life, and giving to get rich is not generosity but investment. The reward is God’s pleasure, fruit in your own life, a share in what the gift accomplishes, and treasure that lasts. And the deepest motive is not reward at all, but gratitude: we give because God has given us his Son. Gifts given out of love for him delight him, and he delights to reward what he himself has produced in us.

On a Tuesday. Think of the practical help you will give this week: money in the offering, a meal for a neighbour, a lift, an hour of your time. Before you give it, say to God: this is for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My God will supply. One of the letter’s most misused promises. “Supply” is to fill. The Philippians filled Paul’s need at real cost to themselves; now God will fill theirs, from resources that cannot run out. And the possessive matters: my God, the God Paul has proved in plenty and want.

Every need. Not every want, request or ambition, but every true need, material and spiritual.

According to his riches. Not merely out of his riches, which would mean a gift drawn from a large supply, but according to them: in proportion to his infinite wealth. God’s supply is measured not by the size of your emergency but by the extent of his glory.

In Christ Jesus. Every provision comes through Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3), and whose riches Paul calls unsearchable (Ephesians 3:8). The logic of Romans 8:32 runs underneath: a Father who has already handed over his own Son for us will not turn stingy over bread and strength and the help of a friend. The deepest need any of us has was met before the parcel ever arrived.

Usually with somebody’s name on it. God had just supplied Paul’s need this way, by a church sending one of its own with a gift. God’s supply is rarely a miracle delivered privately; it usually arrives with somebody’s name on it.

Where Christians differ: a promise of prosperity? This verse is sometimes used to promise wealth to those who give, especially to particular ministries. This commentary’s view: the promise is that God will meet every need of his generous people, not that he will make them rich. Paul himself, who wrote this, knew hunger (v. 12). God supplies what we truly need to live and serve him, sometimes abundantly, sometimes just enough, always faithfully (Matthew 6:31–33). The promise is especially for those, like the Philippians, who give sacrificially to the gospel. Pressing it into the shape of a prosperity promise has wounded a great many people who then concluded that God had broken his word or that their faith had failed.

But what of Christians who really do go hungry? Paul himself knew hunger and thirst, often without food (2 Corinthians 11:27), and he says he had learned to face plenty and hunger (4:12). The promise is not that a believer will never lack bread. It is that God will give him all he truly needs to do God’s will and reach glory, and that he often does it through his people, as he did here through the Philippians. That is why the promise is also a summons: the church is one of the ways God keeps it. If you have plenty, a hungry brother may be waiting for God to answer his prayer through you.

How do I tell a need from a want? A need is what you truly require to live, to do God’s will and to grow in Christ: daily bread, clothing, shelter, strength, wisdom, forgiveness, his presence. A want is what you would like beyond that. God often gives us wants as well, generously, and we may ask him for them. But he does not promise them. A useful test: would I still be able to trust, obey and serve God without this? If yes, it is not a need in this verse’s sense. Asking the question honestly is often the beginning of contentment.

verseByVerse.quote: To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A doxology. Not after the hymn of chapter 2, but after a discussion of church finances. The subject has climbed from a parcel, to a sacrifice, to the riches of glory, that by verse 20 there is nowhere left for it to go except straight up into praise.

Our God and Father. My God (v. 19) widens to our. The imprisoned apostle and the poor congregation who paid for his upkeep stand in the same relation to the same Father.

Glory forever and ever. Glory is the display of his worth. Forever and ever is literally to the ages of the ages, language reaching for a length it cannot state. Against a trial, a quarrel and a gift months in arriving, all temporary, the glory is not.

Where the argument ends. Structurally, the letter’s argument ends here, before the greetings, and it finishes in the same place the hymn of chapter 2 finished: with glory going to God the Father (2:11). Paul has now brought both the descent of the Son and a gift from Macedonia to rest at the same address.

Amen. The word the congregation would say out loud when the letter was read to them. A letter that began with grace and peace has arrived, by way of a prison and a quarrel and a gift, at a room full of people saying amen together.

Through him we say amen. And they say it through Christ. All the promises of God find their Yes in him, Paul told the Corinthians, and that is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). The promise of verse 19 was made in Christ Jesus; the Amen of verse 20 is the church saying yes to it in him. Christ is the Father’s guarantee that the supply will come, and the reason the glory goes back to the Father when it does.

How can I give glory to God when my needs are not being met? Paul wrote this doxology in chains, with hunger not far behind him, so his praise was not the overflow of comfortable circumstances. Glory to God does not mean pretending all is well. It means confessing that he is worthy whatever is happening: that he is good, that his promises stand, that Christ is enough. The psalmists and prophets often praise in the middle of lament (Psalm 42:11; Habakkuk 3:17–18). Begin with what is true of him and what he has already done, above all in Christ. Praise offered in the dark is not less real than praise in the light; it may be the most precious kind.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every saint. Two of those saints are not speaking to each other, and he will not let the greeting skip anyone. Saint means here what it meant in 1:1: not the notably holy, but everyone who is in Christ.

The brothers who are with me. The clause softens the harsh word of 2:21, that they all seek their own interests. Paul was not alone, and it is fair to let the greeting temper the complaint.

Caesar’s household. The phrase did not mean the imperial family; it was the standing term for the vast staff of the palace and the imperial administration: secretaries, accountants, cooks, couriers, most of them slaves or freedmen. Some of them were Christians. Paul is in chains because of Caesar, and the gospel has walked into Caesar’s own house: the receipt for 1:12.

What it meant in Philippi. Hear that read aloud in a Roman colony full of retired legionaries, proud of its tie to Rome, where confessing Jesus as Lord could set you against the emperor’s cult. Christ has subjects in Caesar’s own house. The colony of heaven is bigger than they thought, and it reaches further up the road than anyone would have guessed.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul’s last word gives the full title of the one every tongue will confess (2:11). Grace is not a substance handed out from a store; it is his own kindness, the favour of the one who emptied himself and went to the cross. And it is to be with your spirit, one spirit for a whole church, as if the quarrelling, anxious, generous congregation had a single inner life under his grace. The letter opened with grace (1:2) and closes with it, a frame, not a formality: everything between stands inside grace. (Some manuscripts add Amen.)

Should Christians seek positions of influence? Christians may serve in government, business and every lawful calling, and they should do so faithfully, as salt and light. Joseph served Pharaoh, Daniel served Babylon, and these believers served Caesar. But consider who they were: mostly slaves and freedmen, not the powerful. The gospel did not reach Caesar’s house by Christians seizing power, but by a prisoner in chains talking to his guards. Seek to be faithful where God has put you, high or low. Influence is a stewardship, not a goal, and the kingdom of God advances most often through ordinary faithfulness in unlikely places.
verseByVerse.note: “Caesar’s household” means the emperor’s staff of slaves and freedmen, not his family.
